events.text: {npc} finds you after {debt_years} years. "You {debt}. I have no silver worth giving. But I have this." It is a map, drawn on goatskin, of a valley in the western hills, with a pagoda and a cross.

effects.log: {npc} looks relieved. "It was my grandfather's. Nobody in my family was brave enough. Or foolish enough."

choices.text: Accept, and ask {npc} to come along

mem.note: asked me to come to the valley

effects.log: {npc} hesitates, then grins. "Somebody has to carry the shovel."

choices.text: Refuse: the debt was never for payment

effects.log: {npc} stares, then puts the map in the fire. "Then neither is this." You watch the pagoda burn, a little sorry.

events.text: You have reached the valley on {npc}'s map. The pagoda is real, half fallen, overgrown with vines. Under the cross on the map, there is a stone slab with a carved inscription and an iron ring. {npc} is beside you, pale with excitement.

ok.log: Under it, a chest: old silver, a rusted sword and a letter. You split the silver. {npc} takes the letter and goes very quiet.

fail.log: The slab slips and crushes your toe. Under it, a smaller chest than you hoped, and a letter.

effects.log: "Here lies what I took. Whoever finds it, give it back." There is a name. A village. A date seventy years ago.
{npc} goes back alone next year. You hear only that {npc} came back changed.

events.text: The letter under the pagoda slab was a confession: {npc}'s grandfather was a bandit, and the silver belongs to a village down the valley that was robbed seventy years ago. {npc} has found the village. It is still there, still poor.

choices.text: Return the silver to the village with {npc}

mem.note: returned my grandfather's silver with me

effects.log: The village elder weeps. A shrine goes up: "To the grandchild of the thief, who paid." {npc} stands beside it a long time.

choices.text: Keep your share and let {npc} decide about the rest

effects.log: {npc} returns all of it, including what was yours, out of {his} own pocket. You never quite feel right about it.

choices.text: Find a way to build the village a well instead

effects.log: A well is better than silver. The village has water for the first time in seventy years. {npc} digs every day.

events.text: {npc} turns up at your gate with a pack, a spear and a frown. "You {debt}. I will guard you until I have paid it back with my life or something equal." {npc} sits down on your step. {npc} is not moving.

effects.log: {npc} follows you everywhere, scowling at shopkeepers. Your purse has never been safer, or your privacy less.

ok.log: {npc} agrees to guard you from a distance. A distance of three steps.

fail.log: {npc} refuses. "A debt is a debt." The spear stays on your step.

effects.log: {npc} guards your house, chops your wood and frightens a debt collector. It is almost worth it.

events.text: Your bodyguard has guarded you from: a pickpocket, a goose, a rival's insult, two suitors and a very small dog. Last night {npc} challenged a tavern to a fight for laughing at your hat. Your neighbours have started calling {npc} your shadow.

mem.note: was told the debt is paid

effects.log: "Not yet," says {npc}. "I will know." You go on being guarded.
You teach {npc} to bow and to say good morning. {npc} learns, reluctantly, and becomes a slightly more polite shadow.

choices.text: Go somewhere dangerous to give {npc} a chance

ok.log: You lead your bodyguard into bandit country. {npc} fights like a tiger. It is the happiest you have ever seen anyone.

fail.log: The bandits are many. {npc} carries you out on one shoulder, delighted.

events.text: In a narrow street in the night market, a knife comes for your back. You never see it. {npc} does, and takes it in the arm, and puts the attacker down. Sitting in the gutter, bleeding, {npc} looks up at you, almost happy. "There. Now we are even."

effects.log: You bind the arm. In the morning {npc}'s pack is by the gate. {npc} hugs you, very awkwardly, and leaves for home.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to stay anyway, as a friend

mem.note: asked me to stay as a friend

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it for a long time. "Without a debt?" {npc} stays. The spear goes in the corner. It is better.

choices.text: Find out who sent the knife

ok.log: It was a creditor of a creditor. You deal with it. {npc}, bandaged, insists on coming.

fail.log: You find nothing. {npc} stays a month longer, just in case, and then goes home.

events.text: {npc} has come to tell you, gravely, that the debt for when you {debt_of} is far too large to pay at once. So {npc} will pay one copper coin a year, every year, for the rest of {his} life, with a letter. The first copper is on the table.

effects.log: You put the copper in a box. {npc} bows and goes. You think it is a joke.

choices.text: Insist on giving the copper back

mem.note: tried to give back my copper

effects.log: {npc} refuses with great dignity. The copper stays.

choices.text: Ask for the letters, not the coppers

effects.log: {npc} looks surprised, then pleased. "Both," {npc} says.

events.text: Another copper, another letter from {npc}. The letters have grown. This year's is four pages: the harvest, a quarrel with a neighbour, a bad back, a new grandchild, and at the end, as always: "One copper. Still owing."

effects.log: You write back four pages too. You find you had a great deal to say.

choices.text: Send a copper back with your letter

effects.log: The next letter says: "Now you owe me. This is outrageous."

choices.text: Keep the letters, unanswered, in the box with the coppers

effects.log: The box is getting heavy. You read the letters some nights.

events.text: The coppers keep coming, with letters, every year. Your box is half full. This year's letter is short, and the hand is shaky: {npc} has been ill, and is afraid the payments might stop, and wants you to know that the debt is not forgotten.

mem.note: came to see me when I was ill

effects.log: You go, with the box. {npc} counts the coppers aloud from the bed, delighted, and gets better partly out of sheer pride.
You pay 30 taels for the best physician in the county. Next year the copper comes as usual.

choices.text: Write that the debt is paid in full

effects.log: {npc} writes back: "Not for you to say." The copper comes.

events.text: No copper this year. Instead, a young person comes to your door: {npc}'s grandchild, with a letter and a single copper. "My grandparent died this spring," the grandchild says. "The letter says: one copper. Still owing. I am to keep paying."

choices.text: Accept, and invite the grandchild in

effects.log: You show the grandchild the box, and the letters, and a whole life in coppers. The grandchild cries. You do too.

choices.text: Tell the grandchild the debt ends here

effects.log: You give the grandchild the box of coppers, all of them. "Your grandparent paid in full. Buy something foolish."

choices.text: Accept, and send one copper back every year

effects.log: The grandchild sends one. You send one. It goes on for years.

events.text: {npc} has nothing, {npc} says, but one thing: an old hermit on Mount Bai who once taught {npc}'s father, and who has never taken another student. {npc} has written a letter. "You {debt}. Take this to the hermit. I cannot promise more than a door."

choices.text: Take the letter to Mount Bai

effects.log: You climb for six days. The hermit's hut is a ruin with a fire in it. The hermit reads the letter, snorts, and shuts the door.

mem.note: asked me to come to Mount Bai

effects.log: {npc} comes. The hermit opens the door, sees {npc}, says "You got old," and lets you both in for tea, but not for teaching.

choices.text: Refuse: you do not need a teacher

effects.log: {npc} takes the letter back, hurt, and says no more about it.

events.text: The hermit of Mount Bai has made you sit outside the hut every day for a month. On the thirtieth day the hermit sets you a task: carry water from the spring at the bottom of the mountain to the top, in a bucket with a hole, until the jar is full.

ok.log: You carry water for a month. On the last day you realise you have learned to run without spilling. The hermit nods once.

fail.log: You carry water until you collapse. The hermit watches you from the door and says nothing.

effects.log: You plug the hole with clay. The hermit laughs for the first time. "The last one carried water for three years."

mem.note: wrote to me from Mount Bai

effects.log: {npc} writes back: "My father mended the bucket too, and was thrown off the mountain for being clever. Try something else."

events.text: The hermit of Mount Bai has decided. You may stay one season and learn one thing. "Your friend {npc} paid me for this, forty years ago, with a debt of {npc}'s own. Now it is paid. Choose."

effects.log: The hermit's sword is slow, simple and impossible to beat. You learn a quarter of it. It is enough to change everything.
The hermit's breathing is like a river under ice. You will live longer for it.

"Nothing," says the hermit. "{npc} was thrown off the mountain like the father. The debt was for my life: your friend saved me from bandits once, and asked only that I teach someone worth it." You learn a great deal that season, and most of it is not about swords.

events.text: {npc} has come to repay you in the only way {npc} knows: by cooking. "You {debt}. I will cook for you for one year." {npc} has brought pots. The pots are already on your stove.

effects.log: The first meal is braised pork in black vinegar, and you nearly weep. It goes on like that.
One meal. Eleven dishes. You cannot move until morning.
{npc} takes the pots and goes. You smell braised pork from somewhere for a week.

events.text: {npc}'s cooking has made you famous in a way you did not expect: your house is now where the county's officials want to be invited. Someone has offered {npc} a post as cook to the prefect, and {npc} has refused, "because the debt is not paid."

choices.text: Tell {npc} to take the prefect's post

mem.note: sent me to the prefect's kitchen

effects.log: {npc} takes it. Within a year the prefect is fat and kind. {npc} sends you a dish every festival.
{npc} stays, grumbling happily. The prefect sends someone to steal the recipe for the pork.

mem.note: opened an eating house with me

ok.log: The Grateful Pot opens by the river and is full from the first night. You split the takings.

mem.note: opened an eating house with me

fail.log: The eating house floods in the spring rains. You lose 20 taels and gain a story.

events.text: {npc} has a secret: before cooking, {npc} was a soldier, and deserted, and the army has never stopped looking. An officer has come to the county with a list, and {npc}'s name is on it.

effects.log: You hide {npc} in the cellar for a week. The officer eats at your table, praises the cooking and leaves, none the wiser.

mem.note: spoke to the officer for me

ok.log: The officer, it turns out, was in the same army and remembers the battle {npc} fled. "Half of us ran," the officer says. The name is crossed off.

mem.note: spoke to the officer for me

fail.log: The officer will not listen. {npc} is gone by morning. A dish comes to you every festival, from a different county each year.

effects.log: The officer takes {npc}. You eat cold food for a year.

events.text: {npc} presses a jade pendant into your hands, the colour of deep water, carved with a coiled dragon. "You {debt}. This is the finest thing I have ever owned." It is far finer than {npc} could ever have afforded.

effects.log: You wear it. People stare. A jeweller in the market offers you a fortune for it and then, looking more closely, goes pale.

mem.note: told me where the jade came from

ok.log: {npc} hesitates, then admits it was "found" in a ruined manor. Found, in the sense of taken.

mem.note: asked where my gift came from

fail.log: {npc} is offended. "It is a gift." You accept it, uneasy.

effects.log: {npc} takes it back, deeply hurt, and sells it in another county. You hear that the buyer was arrested.

events.text: A steward from the Lu family manor has come to your door with two guards. The dragon jade you were given belongs to the Lu family, and was stolen in the spring. The steward would like it back, and would like to know who gave it to you.

choices.text: Return it, and do not name {npc}

mem.note: kept my name out of it

effects.log: The steward is not satisfied. The guards search your house. Nothing is found, because there is nothing else to find.

mem.note: named me to the Lu steward

effects.log: The steward thanks you coldly. {npc} is arrested within the week, and sends you no message from the jail.

choices.text: Offer to buy it from the Lu family

effects.log: The steward, surprised, takes 100 taels and lets you keep the jade, now honestly yours. The steward does not ask any more questions.

events.text: {npc} has heard what happened with the Lu steward, and has come to you ashamed. "I wanted to give you something worthy. I gave you trouble instead. Let me pay that back, too."

choices.text: Tell {npc} the honest gift is enough

effects.log: {npc} brings you, the next day, a bag of chestnuts from {his} own tree. They are the best chestnuts you have ever eaten.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to go to the Lu family and apologise

effects.log: {npc} goes. The Lu family, astonished, gives {npc} work in their garden. In a year {npc} is head gardener.

choices.text: Take {npc} on as an honest apprentice

effects.log: {npc} works for you for a year. It is not easy. It is honest. At the end {npc} owns a good coat that nobody has to ask about.

events.text: {npc} arrives at night, out of breath. "You {debt}. Listen to me now: a fever is coming down the river. My cousin in Linjiang says it is the bad kind. You have a week before it reaches here. Get out, or get ready."

effects.log: You leave for the hills with what you can carry. The fever comes. You hear of it from afar.

choices.text: Get ready, and warn the town

ok.log: The town listens. Wells are boiled, the sick are kept apart, the physicians are fetched early. When the fever comes it is held to a corner of the river quarter.

fail.log: The town laughs. You get your own house ready. When the fever comes, people come to your door, and you are glad you were ready.

effects.log: The fever comes. You are lucky. Many are not.

events.text: The fever has reached the river quarter. {npc}, who warned you, has stayed to nurse the sick in the temple, and has sent word asking if you can spare anything: rice, cloth, hands.

choices.text: Go and help in the temple

ok.log: You boil water and carry bowls for a month. The fever breaks. You come out thinner and kinder.

fail.log: You catch it. {npc} nurses you in the corner of the temple. You both live.

effects.log: You send 40 taels of rice and linen. {npc} writes that it saved a street.
You keep away. {npc} comes out of the temple a month later, alive, thin, and looks at you without blame, which is worse.

events.text: The temple where {npc} nursed the fever has put up a tablet with the names of those who helped. {npc}'s is not on it: {npc} asked them to leave it off. "They should remember the fever," {npc} says, "not me."

effects.log: The abbot adds it, small. {npc} pretends to be angry and visits it every spring.
The tablet stays as it is. You and {npc} go every year to burn incense for the names on it.

choices.text: Add your own name, and leave a blank beside it

effects.log: A blank space beside your name. Everybody in the quarter knows whose it is.

events.text: {npc} brings you a little silk purse with seven black seeds inside. "You {debt}. These are snow lotus seeds from the high passes. It took me three years to find them. Plant them where it is cold, and wait."
events.arc: The Seeds of the Snow Lotus

choices.text: Plant them on the north side of the mountain

effects.log: You plant all seven in the snow line and mark the spot with a cairn. Then you wait.

choices.text: Plant them in pots, in a cold cellar

effects.log: You fuss over seven pots for a winter. Nothing happens. You keep fussing.
An herbalist pays 60 taels for them. {npc} hears, and never brings you anything again.

events.text: One of the snow lotus seeds has sprouted. Just one: a thin white shoot in the snow. {npc} has come to see it, kneeling in the cold beside you, breathing on it to keep it warm.
events.arc: The Seeds of the Snow Lotus

effects.log: You build a small screen of stones. You visit every day. {npc} comes every third day with a blanket for it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} how to care for it

effects.log: {npc} knows a great deal about snow lotuses, it turns out, having almost died finding them. You learn about cold, patience and the high passes.

choices.text: Leave it to grow on its own

effects.log: You stop fussing. The lotus does better without you. So, perhaps, do most things.

events.text: The snow lotus has bloomed: a single white flower in the snow, the kind that physicians and cultivators would cross provinces for. {npc} sits beside it with you at dawn.
events.arc: The Seeds of the Snow Lotus

effects.log: It tastes of snow and light. You feel years come back into your bones.

mem.note: gave the lotus back to me

effects.log: {npc} weeps. "It was supposed to be for you." "It was," you say. {npc} gives it to a dying child in the village.

choices.text: Save its seeds and plant a whole field

effects.log: In ten years there is a small white field on the north slope. Physicians come from three provinces. {npc} tends it in old age.

events.text: {npc} hands you a paper crane, carefully folded. "You {debt}. I cannot repay you. I will send you one of these every year, on this day, so that you know I have not forgotten." It is a strange, small thing. It is very well folded.

choices.text: Keep the crane on your shelf

effects.log: It sits on your shelf. Every time you look at it, you feel oddly cared for.
Yours is lopsided. {npc} keeps it anyway, delighted.

choices.text: Say a crane is too little

mem.note: said a crane was too little

effects.log: {npc} goes red and takes it back. No cranes come. You feel, years later, that you were a fool.

events.text: The cranes have come every year on the day. This year's is not paper but thin beaten silver, folded with great difficulty. A note: "I am doing well now. The cranes will get better."

effects.log: {npc} writes back a long letter about a trading house, a small fortune and a spouse. The silver crane goes on the shelf beside the paper ones.

choices.text: Send the silver crane back, and ask for paper

effects.log: The next year, a paper crane comes. Folded inside, very small, a note: "Thank you. I was afraid the paper was not enough."
It is worth 15 taels. You never quite stop being ashamed of it.

events.text: No crane came this year. You wait a month. Then a parcel arrives: a hundred paper cranes, strung on a cord, and a note in a young hand. "My parent {npc} folded these over the last winter, ill, one a day. For all the years to come."

effects.log: A hundred cranes, turning in the light. You will never get through them all. You open one a year.

choices.text: Visit the grave with a crane of your own

effects.log: Your crane is lopsided. You leave it on the stone. A wind takes it up the hill, and you let it go.
You tell {npc}'s child the whole story. The child writes back, and the next year sends a crane, badly folded, and the year after, a better one.

events.text: {npc} draws you aside in the market. "You {debt}. I have joined the Black Gate Sect, the one that has been pressing on the towns of the valley. Nobody knows I owe you. If you want to know what they plan, I will tell you. Once a year. It may be the end of me."
events.arc: The Friend Inside the Black Gate

effects.log: {npc} nods once and disappears into the crowd. The first note comes a month later, folded into a sesame cake.

choices.text: Refuse: it is too dangerous for {npc}

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "You are the only person who has ever said that." {npc} leaves the Black Gate the next spring.

choices.text: Accept, and promise to get {npc} out when it is over

effects.log: "Do not promise," says {npc}. "Just do it."

events.text: A sesame cake comes, with a note folded inside: the Black Gate Sect will raid the market town at the Lantern Festival, when the guards are drunk. {npc}'s hand is shaking on the page.
events.arc: The Friend Inside the Black Gate

ok.log: The guard is sober and ready. The raid fails. The Black Gate begins to look for whoever talked.

fail.log: The guard half listens. The raid is beaten off, barely, with losses.

choices.text: Gather fighters and ambush the raiders

ok.log: You meet the raiders in the bamboo outside town. They never reach the lanterns.

fail.log: You and your fighters hold them in the bamboo, but at a cost.

effects.log: The raid comes. The town suffers. {npc}'s cover is safe. You live with it.

events.text: {npc} has been found out. A last sesame cake came, with no note, only a bloodstain and a place: the old quarry, at dawn. The Black Gate will execute {npc} there as a traitor.
events.arc: The Friend Inside the Black Gate

mem.note: came to the quarry for me

ok.log: You come over the quarry rim at dawn. The executioners scatter. You carry {npc} down the hill, and {npc} weeps all the way.

mem.note: came to the quarry for me

fail.log: You get {npc} out, and nearly die doing it. You lie in a farmhouse for a month, side by side, healing.

choices.text: Bargain with the Black Gate for {npc}'s life

effects.log: You pay 150 taels. The Black Gate sells {npc} back, beaten and alive, and never troubles the valley again, for reasons you do not ask.

choices.text: Bring the town guard and the valley militia

mem.note: brought the valley to the quarry

ok.log: Three hundred farmers with hoes appear over the quarry rim. The Black Gate runs.

fail.log: The militia is too late. {npc} escaped alone, by a miracle, and comes to your door a month later.

events.text: {npc} takes you to an empty threshing floor at dusk. "You {debt}. My teacher's family has one move, the Falling Crane, that has never been taught to an outsider. I will teach it to you." {npc} shows you the first half. Then stops. "That is all I know. My teacher died before the rest."

effects.log: The first half is beautiful and useless: it leaves you wide open. You practise it anyway.

choices.text: Ask who else might know the rest

mem.note: asked about the rest of the move

effects.log: {npc} thinks. "My teacher had a sister who left for the south. That was thirty years ago."

choices.text: Decline: a family move should stay in the family

effects.log: {npc} bows, moved. "Then I will keep it for someone of the family, if any are left."

events.text: {npc} has news: the teacher's sister is alive, very old, in a fishing village in the south, and has agreed to see "the one who learned half." {npc} cannot travel. You must go alone.

mem.note: went south for the Falling Crane

ok.log: The old sister watches your half move and laughs: the second half is the first half, done backwards. You will never fight the same way again.

fail.log: The old sister watches your half move in silence and promises to think about it. You stay a month, mending nets.

effects.log: The sister writes back three characters: "Show me." You go.

choices.text: Send {npc} the money to go instead

effects.log: You pay 40 taels for {npc}'s journey. {npc} comes back with the whole move and teaches it to you in the threshing floor at dusk, both halves.

events.text: The Falling Crane, complete, has become your best move. {npc} comes to watch you practise it one evening, and asks a question that has clearly been waiting years: "Will you teach it to someone, when you are old? It should not die with us."

mem.note: promised to pass on the Crane

effects.log: You promise. {npc} looks satisfied in a way you have never seen. "Then the debt is paid," {npc} says. "All of it."

choices.text: Teach it to {npc}'s best student now

mem.note: taught the Crane to my student

effects.log: The student is clumsy and stubborn. Perfect. {npc} watches every lesson.
You write it all down, both halves, in a plain hand. {npc} reads it and corrects one word.

events.text: {npc} has made a song about you, as repayment. "You {debt}. I am no fighter. But I can sing." The song is about the time you {debt_of}, and it is, against all odds, very catchy.

effects.log: You thank {npc}. You also hum it all evening without meaning to.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to change the bad rhyme

mem.note: asked me to fix the rhyme

effects.log: {npc} changes it. The new rhyme is worse. You prefer it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} not to sing it in public

mem.note: asked me not to sing it

effects.log: {npc} agrees, a little sad. You sometimes hum it alone.

events.text: The song has spread. You hear it in three teahouses, sung by strangers. In each one it is a little different: in the third, you rescued a princess, killed a tiger and are seven feet tall.

effects.log: {npc} is mortified. "I only sang it twice!" Songs, you both learn, have their own legs.
The singers do not want to be corrected. A seven-foot hero is better business.
Doors open for you. Innkeepers give you the good room. You begin, slightly, to believe the tiger.

events.text: A real tiger has come down to the village at the foot of the hills, and the villagers have sent for you, because the song says you have killed one. {npc} arrives first, pale, with a spear: "This is my fault. I am coming."

mem.note: faced the real tiger with me

ok.log: It is a long, terrible night. In the morning the tiger is dead and the song is true. {npc} adds a verse, in which {npc} is holding the spear.

mem.note: faced the real tiger with me

fail.log: The tiger leaves you both badly hurt and runs into the hills. The song now has a sad verse. It is the best one.

choices.text: Drive the tiger off with fire

mem.note: drove off the tiger with me

ok.log: Torches and drums all night. The tiger goes back to the deep forest. The song gets a new verse, in which you are clever instead of seven feet tall.

fail.log: The tiger is not afraid of fire. You both climb a tree and wait for the hunters.

effects.log: You confess you have never killed a tiger. The villagers hire real hunters. {npc} writes a new song, about honesty. It does not catch on.

events.text: {npc} has heard that you owe money to the Yang brothers, who collect with clubs. "You {debt}. Let me deal with the Yangs." {npc} cracks {his} knuckles, which is alarming, because {npc} is a clerk.

effects.log: {npc} goes to the Yang brothers with a ledger. You wait, worried, for three hours.

mem.note: went to the Yangs with me

effects.log: You go together. The Yangs are very large. {npc} opens the ledger.
You pay 50 taels. {npc} is clearly disappointed, having practised a speech.

events.text: {npc} has gone through the Yang brothers' ledgers, line by line, and found that they have been charging interest on interest for ten years. Half the town has been paying them three times over. {npc} has the proof and is terrified.

choices.text: Take the proof to the magistrate with {npc}

mem.note: took the Yangs to the magistrate with me

ok.log: The magistrate is impressed. The Yangs are fined and their debts cancelled. Half the town comes to thank {npc}, who hides.

mem.note: went to the magistrate with me

fail.log: The magistrate is the Yangs' cousin. You leave fast. The Yangs are now looking for {npc}.

choices.text: Use the proof to make the Yangs cancel your debt and nobody else's

effects.log: The Yangs cancel your debt, sweating. {npc} looks at you differently afterwards.
{npc} is safe and furious. "I was not afraid," {npc} says, shaking.

events.text: The Yang brothers are out of business, and {npc}, the clerk who brought them down, has become the most trusted person in town: people bring {npc} their contracts to read before signing. {npc} has opened a small office and has hung a sign that says: "Debts Read Here. First Reading Free for the One Who Started This."

effects.log: There is a chair with your name on it. You sit in it. {npc} reads you a contract, for fun, very fast.
You send everyone you know. {npc} is soon too busy to sleep and too happy to mind.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read your own contracts

effects.log: {npc} finds two traps in your rent and one in your sword-polisher's bill. You save 30 taels a year.

events.text: {npc} has had a child, and arrives with a red egg and an announcement: "You {debt}. We have named the child after you." The baby is red, furious and, apparently, now yours in name.

effects.log: The baby sneezes on you. {npc} takes this as a blessing.

choices.text: Give a silver lock for the baby

mem.note: gave the baby a silver lock

effects.log: You give a silver longevity lock worth 20 taels. {npc} hangs it on the cradle and tells everyone.
{npc} considers your suggestion, and names the next child that instead.

events.text: The child named after you is eight, and has been told the story of you by {npc} every night since birth. The child arrives at your door with {npc}, very serious, to ask if you are really as good as the stories.

choices.text: Show the child a little sword

effects.log: The child watches with enormous eyes and goes home and practises with a stick until supper.

choices.text: Tell the child the truth: you are not

effects.log: The child thinks about it and says, "Then I will be." {npc} looks at you over the child's head, proud and alarmed.

choices.text: Give the child a small task to do

effects.log: You ask the child to carry a cup of water across the courtyard without spilling. The child spills. Tries again. Tries again.

events.text: The child named after you is grown, and has entered the jianghu, and has sent you a letter through {npc}: there is trouble on the Southern Road, a gang of kidnappers, and the young one intends to deal with it alone, "as you would."

ok.log: You arrive in time to fight beside the young one. Afterwards, the young one is furious: "I had it in hand." You did not. It is good to see your name do well.

fail.log: You get there. It is close. The young one carries you out, which is the right way round, eventually.

effects.log: The young one waits, grumbling, and goes with the county guard. Everyone comes back. {npc} sends you a whole roast duck.
The young one deals with it, alone, as you would have. The stories about the two of you get muddled in the teahouses.

events.text: {npc} has become the ferryman at the White Stone crossing, and has made you a promise: "You {debt}. As long as I hold this pole, you will never pay to cross." It is a small thing. The river is wide.

effects.log: You cross for free. {npc} insists on carrying your bag up the far bank, too.
{npc} takes the copper and throws it in the river. You stop insisting.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to carry the poor free instead

mem.note: gave my promise to the poor

effects.log: {npc} looks at you and nods. A sign goes up: "Free for the hungry, by request of a friend."

events.text: Floods. The White Stone crossing is the only way across the river for fifty miles, and the water is rising. A village on the far bank is cut off, and {npc} is the only ferryman willing to try.

ok.log: You row six times across. The last time, the boat goes over in the shallows. Everyone lives, including the village's one cow.

fail.log: The boat turns over on the third crossing. You save two children and {npc} saves you.

ok.log: A rope line across the river lets the boat be hauled. Nobody drowns.

fail.log: The rope breaks. {npc} rows anyway, alone, and makes it.

effects.log: {npc} goes. Of course {npc} goes. You stand on the bank all night.

events.text: {npc} is too old to hold the pole now, and has passed the White Stone ferry to a grandchild. The grandchild has been told of the promise and meets you at the landing with a bow: "You will never pay to cross."

effects.log: {npc} sits on the bank under a straw hat and waves at you all the way across.

choices.text: Ask that the promise go to the poor instead, as before

effects.log: The sign is repainted. The grandchild adds a line: "And to anyone who says please."

choices.text: Sit with {npc} on the bank instead of crossing

mem.note: sat on the bank with me

effects.log: You do not cross. You sit with {npc} all afternoon and watch the boat go back and forth.

events.text: {npc} gives you a small iron token stamped with a coin. "You {debt}. Show this at any branch of the Qian trading house and they will lend you up to five hundred taels, once, no questions. I have arranged it." It feels heavy for its size.

effects.log: You sew it into your coat. You feel, for the first time in a long while, safe.

choices.text: Use it at once, for something you have always wanted

effects.log: You take two hundred taels and buy a horse, a sword and a feast. Later you will remember the word "once."

choices.text: Return it: you do not borrow

effects.log: {npc} takes it back, impressed and disappointed.

events.text: You hear that the Qian trading house is in trouble. The one who arranged your iron token, {npc}, has put up {his} own house as surety for the tokens. If one more token is called in this month, {npc} is ruined.

choices.text: Bring your token back, unused, so {npc} can cancel it

effects.log: {npc} weeps with relief. The house survives the month. {npc} is careful about promises after that.

mem.note: lent me silver when the Qian house failed

effects.log: You lend 80 taels. The house survives. {npc} pays you back with interest you refuse.

choices.text: Call in your token anyway: you need it

effects.log: You take two hundred taels. {npc} loses the house. You both know why.

events.text: The Qian trading house has recovered, and {npc} has become its senior partner. A letter comes with a new iron token, this one gold-plated: "No limit. Never called in. Do not argue."

effects.log: You keep it in a box and never use it. Knowing it is there is the whole of its value.
"The first one was enough," you write. {npc} hangs your letter in the counting room.

choices.text: Use it to fund a school in the poor quarter

mem.note: built the school with the token

effects.log: {npc} is astonished, then delighted, then pays for a second school.

events.text: {npc} leads a grey mule to your gate with a red tassel on its bridle. "You {debt}. This is the best thing I own. The name is Magistrate, because it never moves unless it wants to." Magistrate looks at you. Magistrate does not move.

effects.log: Magistrate eats your hat, your garden and a letter from the county office. You grow fond of it against your will.

choices.text: Accept, and try to ride it

ok.log: You ride Magistrate to market in half a day. Magistrate is impressed. So are you.

fail.log: Magistrate puts you in a ditch. {npc}, watching, laughs until crying.

choices.text: Refuse: you could not take {npc}'s best thing

effects.log: {npc} looks relieved and leads Magistrate home. Magistrate looks back at you, the only time it ever looks back at anyone.

events.text: Magistrate the mule has stopped dead on the mountain road and will not move, for an hour, in the rain, though you pull and plead and offer apples. Then, ahead of you, the whole road slides down into the valley with a roar.

effects.log: You stand in the rain hugging a wet mule. You will never pull its rope again.
{npc} writes back: "I told you it was the best thing I owned. It did that for me twice."

choices.text: Take the high path home, Magistrate leading

effects.log: Magistrate takes you home by a path you did not know existed. You suspect it has been here before.

events.text: Magistrate the mule is very old, and has stopped eating. {npc} has come to sit with it, and with you, in the stable.

choices.text: Sit up with Magistrate through the night

effects.log: Magistrate puts its head on {npc}'s knee near dawn and goes quietly. You bury it on the hill above the old road.
The horse doctor says it is simply old. Magistrate looks at the doctor with deep contempt and lives another two years.
{npc} takes it home. Magistrate dies there that winter, in its old stable. {npc} writes that it seemed content.

events.text: {npc} has paid the monks of the Temple of Quiet Waters to keep a lamp burning in your name, day and night. "You {debt}. While it burns, the gods will know about you." You did not know the gods needed telling.

choices.text: Visit the temple to see the lamp

effects.log: It is a small bronze lamp in a row of hundreds. Yours has a paper with your name on it, in {npc}'s careful hand.

choices.text: Pay to keep {npc}'s lamp burning too

effects.log: You pay 10 taels. Two lamps side by side. The monks think it is very funny.

mem.note: said there was no need for the lamp

effects.log: "There is every need," says {npc}, and goes on paying.

events.text: A fire at the Temple of Quiet Waters. Half the lamp hall is gone. A monk comes to tell you that yours survived, alone, at the end of a blackened row. {npc} has already gone to the temple to help rebuild.

effects.log: You carry beams for a month. {npc} carries more and complains less. The new lamp hall has your lamp in its centre.
You pay 60 taels. The abbot puts a stone at the door with your name and {npc}'s together.
You take the little lamp home and keep it burning on your own shelf. {npc} says the gods can find it there.

events.text: The monks of the Temple of Quiet Waters have sent for you: {npc}'s lamp has gone out. And {npc} is gravely ill. The monks are frightened of the omen and ask what to do.

choices.text: Go and light it again yourself

effects.log: You light it. The same night, {npc}'s fever breaks. The monks will never stop telling the story.
You sit by the bed. {npc} wakes and asks about the lamp. You say you lit it. It is the first lie you have ever told {npc}, and the monks, who did light it, forgive you.

choices.text: Tell the monks lamps are only lamps

effects.log: The monks light it anyway. {npc} recovers. You are not sure what you believe.

events.text: A letter from {npc} that makes no sense at all: the price of plums, a cousin's cough, an owl on the roof. At the bottom: "You {debt}. Read it as we read the exam papers." You have no idea what that means.

ok.log: Every third character. It says: "They come at the new moon. North gate. Twenty men." You do not know who "they" are.

fail.log: You get the plums and the owl and nothing else. Then you notice every third character.

effects.log: A retired clerk reads it in a moment. "North gate, new moon, twenty men." The clerk asks no questions.
The new moon comes. So do twenty men, through the north gate. You survive it. You never learn what the letter said.

events.text: The new moon. Twenty masked men come to your door by the north gate, exactly as {npc}'s letter warned. They are hired swords of an enemy you made years ago. You are ready.

ok.log: You hold the narrow gate. Twenty is a lot. You manage. In the morning, the gate is splintered and you are standing.

fail.log: You hold the gate, barely. When the last of them runs you sit down in the mud and do not get up until noon.

choices.text: Leave the house empty and watch

effects.log: They break in and find an empty house and a cold teapot. You watch from the hill, then follow them home.
The guard catches eleven. The rest flee. The magistrate wants to know how you knew.

events.text: {npc} comes to see you, at last, in person. "My employer hired those twenty. I wrote the letter in our old code at night, by one candle. If my employer ever learns, I am dead." {npc} needs to get out of the province, now.

mem.note: got me out of the province

ok.log: A cart of cabbages, a false name, a ferry at night. {npc} writes from three provinces away: "Plums are cheap here."

fail.log: The first plan fails at the ferry. The second works. You have a bruise and a friend in a far province.

effects.log: {npc} takes 60 taels and goes before dawn. You never learn where.

choices.text: Go to {npc}'s employer and end this

ok.log: You end the threat at its source. {npc} does not have to run. You have a new enemy, and one fewer.

fail.log: You fail and run. {npc} runs too, with you. You lie low in the hills for a season, together.

events.text: {npc} arrives with a thin boy of ten, the youngest of {his} children. "You {debt}. I have nothing else. Take Little Shu as your servant. Shu eats little and works hard." The boy is shaking.
events.arc: The Boy Who Was Given to You

choices.text: Take the boy as a student, not a servant

mem.note: took my son as a student

effects.log: You tell {npc} that Shu will learn, not serve. {npc} cannot speak for a long time.
{npc} is relieved and ashamed. Shu looks back at you over one shoulder all the way down the road.

choices.text: Take the boy as a servant

effects.log: Shu works hard and eats little. Too little. You start leaving food where Shu will find it.

events.text: Little Shu is fourteen and has been practising a sword form at night, secretly, by copying you through a crack in the wall. It is clumsy. It is also, in places, better than yours. {npc} has come to visit and has seen it.
events.arc: The Boy Who Was Given to You

effects.log: Shu learns fast. Too fast. You start to worry about what kind of fighter you are making.

choices.text: Send Shu to a proper sect

mem.note: sent my son to a sect

effects.log: You pay 30 taels for Shu's entrance fees. {npc} weeps at the sect gate. Shu does not look back this time.
Shu stops. You find Shu two months later practising in the woods instead.

events.text: Shu is grown, famous, a sword master now, and has come back to the house where Shu first learned. Shu kneels before you and {npc} together. "My father gave me to you to pay a debt. You gave me back a life. I have come to repay both."
events.arc: The Boy Who Was Given to You

choices.text: Raise Shu up and refuse any repayment

effects.log: Shu insists. In the end Shu repays you both by staying a month and fixing the roof.
Shu opens a school in the village. On the wall is a crack, very carefully preserved.

choices.text: Spar with Shu, for old times

ok.log: You win. Shu laughs: "I let you." Shu did not.

fail.log: Shu wins. {npc} cheers, then remembers to look sorry.

events.text: A magistrate's runner stops you at the city gate on a warrant you know nothing about. Before you can argue, {npc} appears, out of breath. "You {debt}. Let me vouch for you." {npc} signs the runner's slate. The runner lets you through, reluctantly.
events.arc: The Name You Were Vouched By

choices.text: Thank {npc} and ask what the warrant was

effects.log: A theft at the salt office, and a witness who says it was someone of your height and your coat. {npc} has put {his} own name on the line for yours.

choices.text: Go to the magistrate at once to clear it

ok.log: The witness, faced with you, admits the thief was shorter. The warrant is torn up.

fail.log: The magistrate is busy. The warrant stays. So does {npc}'s name on it.

effects.log: You leave. {npc}'s name stays on the slate for both of you.

events.text: The salt office theft has been solved, but not in the way you hoped. The real thief has fled, and the magistrate, needing someone, is now looking at the person who vouched for you. {npc} has been summoned.
events.arc: The Name You Were Vouched By

mem.note: stood before the magistrate with me

ok.log: You stand together and argue until the magistrate gives up. You are both fined a day of road sweeping, which you do side by side.

mem.note: stood before the magistrate with me

fail.log: The magistrate fines you both 30 taels for "confusion." You pay both shares.

mem.note: caught the salt thief for me

ok.log: You track the thief to a boat on the river and bring the thief back by the collar.

fail.log: You find the thief and lose the fight. The thief escapes. You crawl back to tell {npc} you tried.

effects.log: {npc} is fined heavily and loses a post. You hear about it later, and it sits badly.

events.text: Something strange: for a year your neighbour, Old Chen the cobbler, has been receiving gifts on the doorstep: ducks, cloth, a whole pig at New Year. Today you catch the giver in the act. It is {npc}, who stares at you, then at Chen's door, then at the duck in {his} hands. "You {debt}. I have been leaving these at the wrong house."

effects.log: {npc} laughs too, helplessly, holding the duck. Old Chen opens the door, sees you both, and closes it again.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to keep giving to Chen

mem.note: told me to keep giving to Chen

effects.log: Old Chen is poor, and it has been a good year for Chen because of {npc}. The gifts go on, to the right wrong house.
{npc} gives you the duck. It is an excellent duck.

events.text: Old Chen the cobbler has worked out who has been leaving the gifts, and has made {npc} a pair of boots of thanks. And then, being a proud man, a pair for you, "for being the reason." The boots are very good.

effects.log: They are the best boots you have ever worn. You walk thirty miles in them without a blister.

choices.text: Bring {npc} and Chen together for dinner

mem.note: had dinner with Chen and me

effects.log: Old Chen talks all evening about shoes. {npc} listens to every word. It is a strange, warm evening.
Chen is offended. You are not forgiven until you buy three more pairs.

events.text: Old Chen the cobbler has died, and left the little shop, with the last, the awl and the ledger, to "the two who mixed up their doorsteps." The ledger has one page on you and one on {npc}: every pair of shoes Chen ever made you, with your foot sizes.

choices.text: Keep the shop open between you

effects.log: You hire a young cobbler and pay the rent between you. The shop's sign still says "Chen."

choices.text: Give the shop to Chen's apprentice

effects.log: The apprentice weeps and keeps the ledger on the wall.
You keep it. {npc} borrows it every year to read the page about your feet.

events.text: {npc}, a goatherd's child grown into a goatherd, takes you up a cliff you have looked at all your life and shows you a path no wider than a foot. "You {debt}. Nobody knows this path but my family and the goats. Now you."

ok.log: At the top you can see three valleys. You understand at once what the path is worth.

fail.log: You slip twice and hold on by your fingers. {npc} talks you up the last stretch.

effects.log: "Over the ridge," says {npc}, "into the valley behind the Iron Gate fort. Every army that has ever wanted that fort would have killed for this path."

mem.note: promised to keep the path secret

effects.log: {npc} looks at you seriously. "Use it once, if you must. Then forget it."

events.text: War has come to the valley. An army is camped before the Iron Gate fort, and the fort will fall within the week. The general of the defenders is looking for anyone who knows another way in. You know {npc}'s goat path.

choices.text: Lead the defenders' relief up the goat path

ok.log: You bring three hundred men up the cliff in the night. The fort holds. The general wants your name. You give it.

fail.log: Halfway up, the outposts see you. It is a bloody climb. The fort holds, at a cost.

effects.log: {npc} says, "This is what it was for." You lead them up together.
The fort falls. The path stays a secret. You never know if you were right.

events.text: After the war, soldiers came looking for the goat path, and found it, and widened it into a road. {npc}'s family's secret is now a highway with a toll gate. {npc} is sitting on the cliff above it, with the last of the goats.

mem.note: sat on the cliff with me

effects.log: You sit together and watch the carts. "Well," says {npc}, "the goats are happy. They never liked the old way."
The general owes you. {npc} becomes toll keeper and lets goats through free.

mem.note: found a new path with me

ok.log: You spend a summer on the cliffs and find one. You do not tell anybody. Neither does {npc}.

fail.log: You find nothing. {npc} says there are no new paths. Only paths nobody has needed yet.

events.text: {npc} lays a long bundle across your table and unwraps it: an old sword, plain hilt, blade like a strip of winter sky. "You {debt}. This has been in my family for nine generations. It is yours." {npc} does not mention that {his} family was not asked.

effects.log: It is a wonderful blade. When you draw it, old soldiers in the street turn their heads.

ok.log: {npc} admits they do not know yet. You agree to keep the sword in trust until they do.

fail.log: {npc} is offended. "It is mine to give." You keep it, uneasy.

choices.text: Refuse: nine generations is too much

effects.log: {npc} takes it home. The family, you hear, is enormously relieved and sends you a ham.

events.text: {npc}'s eldest cousin has arrived at your gate, a stern elder with a stern beard, to request the return of the family sword, given away "by a fool with a good heart." {npc} has come too, red-faced, behind the cousin.

mem.note: gave the sword back to my family

effects.log: The cousin, surprised by your grace, invites you to the family's New Year. {npc} is forgiven, mostly.

choices.text: Propose a duel for it with the cousin

ok.log: You win. The cousin bows and leaves the sword with you, impressed despite the beard.

fail.log: The cousin wins, takes the sword and, privately, thanks you for an honest bout.

choices.text: Offer to buy it from the family

effects.log: The cousin takes 120 taels, coldly. The sword is yours. {npc}'s family uses the silver to repair the ancestral hall, and is a little warmer to you each year.

events.text: {npc}'s family is in trouble: bandits have taken the ancestral hall, and the family's young people cannot drive them out. The stern cousin, older now, sends you a letter: "You know the sword. The sword knows the hall. Will you come?"

choices.text: Go and drive the bandits out

roll.foeName: the bandits in the ancestral hall

ok.log: You walk into the hall with the old sword. The bandits leave by the windows. The cousin hands you the hall key, for a night, as an honour.

fail.log: It is a hard fight. You win it with the young people of the family behind you, which is better.

choices.text: Send the sword back to them, to use

effects.log: The family's young people drive the bandits out with their own sword. The cousin writes: "We did not know we could."
You pay 50 taels. The hall is recovered by strangers. The family is grateful. It is not quite the same.

events.text: {npc} hands you a key and a deed. "You {debt}. My aunt left me a house on Willow Lane. I live in the hills. It is yours." It is a real house, with a real garden. There is, the deed does not mention, already someone living in it.

effects.log: The house is lovely. In the kitchen sits a very old woman with a cat, who looks at you and says, "You must be the new one. Sit down. The tea is ready."
{npc} thinks. "Nobody, as far as I know. Unless Granny Shi stayed on."
You sell it for 150 taels. You later hear the buyer found a tenant who would not leave, and a cat who would not let anyone near the stove.

events.text: Granny Shi, who has lived in the house on Willow Lane for forty years, does not intend to leave. Granny Shi was {npc}'s aunt's companion, and has nowhere else to go. The cat agrees.

choices.text: Let Granny Shi stay, rent free

effects.log: You lodge in the back room. Granny Shi cooks, criticises and tells you everything about everyone on the lane.

mem.note: came to decide about Granny Shi

effects.log: {npc} comes. Granny Shi scolds {npc} for an hour about not visiting. You both end up mending the roof.

choices.text: Insist that Granny Shi must go

effects.log: You insist. Granny Shi goes, with the cat. You have a house, and the lane does not speak to you.

events.text: Granny Shi has died, at a great age, in the house on Willow Lane. The cat is still there. The neighbours have come to tell you, and to see what you will do with the house now.

choices.text: Keep the house and the cat

effects.log: The cat sleeps on your feet. The lane accepts you, eventually, as Granny Shi's lodger.
{npc} moves in. The cat moves onto {npc}'s feet. You visit often.

choices.text: Turn it into a home for old people with nowhere to go

effects.log: You pay 50 taels to fit it out. It fills within a month. The cat runs the place.

events.text: {npc}, now a clerk in the county tax office, leans across the counter. "You {debt}. Your page in the land register has been lost. Quite lost. The fire last year. I am afraid you will have no tax to pay for some time." {npc} winks with both eyes.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Lost a Page

effects.log: No tax collector comes. You save 50 taels this year. Your conscience costs a little more.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to find the page again

mem.note: asked me to find the page

effects.log: {npc} looks at you strangely, and finds the page that afternoon. "I never had anyone ask me that."
You say nothing. The page stays lost. The silence is, somehow, an agreement.

events.text: An auditor from the provincial capital has arrived at the county tax office. The auditor is famous for finding lost pages, and has already found that several are missing, including yours. {npc} has sent you a frightened note.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Lost a Page

choices.text: Go to the auditor and pay what you owe

mem.note: paid before the auditor found me

effects.log: You pay 80 taels of back tax. The auditor, impressed, does not look further into who lost the page. {npc} keeps the post.

choices.text: Help {npc} put the pages back in order before the audit

ok.log: You work all night, two of you, with lamp and brush. The register is perfect. The auditor finds nothing.

fail.log: The pages are fixed badly. The auditor raises an eyebrow and moves on, for now.

effects.log: {npc} is dismissed. You keep the silver. You have lost something else.

events.text: {npc} has left the tax office and become, of all things, an auditor: the most honest and most feared in the province. {npc} has sent you a copy of the auditor's oath, with a note: "You did this."
events.arc: The Clerk Who Lost a Page

effects.log: {npc} writes back: "Your accounts will be audited first. Out of friendship."
It hangs on your wall. Visitors read it and become slightly more careful about their own taxes.

choices.text: Invite {npc} to dinner and pay for it with a receipt

effects.log: {npc} examines the receipt carefully, approves it, and laughs.

events.text: {npc} has finished training as a physician, and says that you, of all people, will never pay for medicine again. "You {debt}. Every illness, every wound, every cough: mine." You have a cough. {npc} has a bag.
events.arc: The Physician Who Will Not Take Silver

effects.log: Bitter, black and awful. The cough is gone by morning. {npc} is insufferable about it.
You leave 10 taels. {npc} finds it and puts it in your tea, which is very difficult to drink.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to treat the poor in your name instead

effects.log: {npc} opens a free clinic one day a week, with your name over the door. You are embarrassed every time you pass it.

events.text: You have been wounded badly. A blade, a fever, and three physicians who shook their heads. {npc} has arrived with the bag and a face like iron, and has sent the other three away.
events.arc: The Physician Who Will Not Take Silver

effects.log: {npc} does not sleep for four days. On the fifth you open your eyes. {npc} is asleep on the floor with a needle in one hand.

mem.note: argued with me on your sickbed

effects.log: You argue about every herb. {npc} is right about all of them. You live.
{npc} tells you: one in three. You decide to be the one. {npc} pretends not to weep when you are.

events.text: {npc} is ill now, and is, of course, a terrible patient: refuses medicine, refuses rest, diagnoses the other physicians. {npc}'s student comes to you in despair. "You are the only one my teacher will listen to."
events.arc: The Physician Who Will Not Take Silver

choices.text: Sit by {npc} and make {npc} drink the medicine

effects.log: You sit there with the bowl until it is drunk. {npc} glares, drinks, sleeps and recovers, and never forgives you for the bowl.
Three people who would be dead without {npc} stand at the bed. {npc} takes the medicine without another word.
It is your turn. You argue about every herb. You are wrong about all of them. {npc} gets better out of sheer exasperation.

events.text: {npc} has come to repay you. You tell {npc}, kindly, that there is no debt: what you did, you did freely. {npc} goes pale. "No debt? You cannot say that. I will not allow it."

effects.log: {npc} leaves in a state of great agitation. You suspect this is not the end of it.

choices.text: Accept a small gift, to make {npc} feel better

effects.log: You accept a jar of pickled turnips. {npc} looks unsatisfied. The turnips are good.
You name twenty taels. {npc} pays it at once, beaming, and walks away lighter. It is the simplest solution, and you feel slightly cheated of a story.

events.text: {npc} has begun repaying the debt you forgave, against your will, in instalments: a goose on your step, a new gate, a poem in the teahouse, your roof mended while you slept. This morning there is a small ox in your courtyard.

effects.log: The ox comes back the next morning, with a bow tied to it.

ok.log: You argue for an hour. {npc} agrees to stop. The next morning, there is a second ox.

fail.log: You lose the argument. You keep the ox. You name it Debt.

effects.log: You send 30 taels. Now {npc} owes you again. The goose returns the next morning.

events.text: You now own two oxen, a goose, a new gate, a mended roof and the best-kept garden in the county, and {npc}, exhausted, has come to sit down on your step. "I give up," {npc} says. "Tell me what you want. Anything."

choices.text: Ask {npc} for one cup of tea, together

mem.note: drank the tea of the forgiven debt

effects.log: You drink tea on the step. "That is all?" "That is all." {npc} laughs until both oxen look over.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to take the oxen back

effects.log: {npc} takes the oxen. And the goose. But not, oddly, the roof.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to forgive a debt of their own, to someone else

effects.log: {npc} goes very quiet. Then goes to a poor cousin, and tears up an IOU. It is the best repayment you could have asked for.

events.text: {npc} sends you a letter from the dry hills of the west. "You {debt}. I have nothing to give you. So I have dug a well in your name, in a village with no water." There is a drawing of the well. There is, in very small characters on the stone, your name.

effects.log: {npc} writes back with a list of who drinks from it. It is a long list.

choices.text: Send silver for a second well

effects.log: You send 40 taels. The second well goes in the next village. It has {npc}'s name on it.

ok.log: You walk west for a month. The well is real. The water is sweet. The village children follow you everywhere.

fail.log: The road is dry and long. The well, when you reach it, is the best drink of your life.

events.text: A drought in the west. The well in your name is the only one in that country that has not run dry, and people are walking three days to reach it. {npc} has written: the village is overwhelmed, and the headman has asked whether the well can be closed to strangers.

choices.text: Write that it must stay open to all

effects.log: The well stays open. People come from three days away. Somehow it holds.

choices.text: Send silver for a second shaft

effects.log: You pay 60 taels. A second shaft is dug. It holds. People still talk about it.
The headman keeps it open in the mornings only. It seems to be enough.

events.text: The village in the west that had no water is now a town, and has sent an invitation by caravan: they would like to name the new market square after the one whose name is on the well, and after {npc}, who dug it.

mem.note: went to the town of the well with me

effects.log: The square is named. There is a feast. You and {npc} drink from the well together, and it is still sweet.

choices.text: Ask that the square be named for {npc} alone

effects.log: It is. {npc} writes: "You are a fraud. I will never forgive you for it."

choices.text: Ask that it be named for the water

effects.log: The square is called Sweet Water. It is the right name.

events.text: {npc} has heard you are in trouble, and has come. You are not in trouble. {npc} looks embarrassed. "You {debt}. I swore that when you needed me I would come. I heard wrong. But I meant it." {npc} looks a lot older than you remember.

effects.log: {npc} stays three days, mends your gate, and tells you all about a life you knew nothing of. On the fourth morning there is a note: "Next time it will be real."

choices.text: Tell {npc} the promise is kept, by coming

effects.log: {npc} shakes {his} head. "Coming is not keeping. I will know when."
{npc} laughs too, and leaves, and you think nothing more of it.

events.text: It is real this time. Enemies at your gate in the snow, more than you can hold. And at the back of their ranks, cutting forward through the night, an old cloaked figure with a sword. It is {npc}, who has walked for eleven days.

mem.note: kept my promise at your gate

ok.log: Back to back by dawn. The gate holds. {npc} sits down in the snow and laughs. "There. Now it is kept."

mem.note: kept my promise at your gate

fail.log: You both bleed for it. The gate holds. {npc} binds your arm and tells you it is kept.

choices.text: Hold the gate and let {npc} take them from behind

ok.log: Caught between, the enemy breaks. {npc} walks in through the gate as if visiting for tea.

fail.log: The plan works too slowly. It works.

effects.log: {npc} does not go back. {npc} has never gone back in {his} life.

events.text: {npc}, who kept the promise at your gate, is very old now and has sent for you, not because of any trouble. Only because, the letter says, {npc} would like to see the one {npc} kept a promise to, once more, before the end.

effects.log: You sit by {npc} through a winter afternoon. {npc} talks about the snow and the gate as though it were the best day of a long life. Perhaps it was. {npc} dies in the night, smiling.

choices.text: Go, and bring the sword from that night

effects.log: {npc} holds the sword one more time, and gives it back. "Keep it for when somebody needs you." {npc} dies that spring.
Your letter arrives the day before {npc} dies. The family says it was read aloud three times.

events.text: {npc} has sent word: the debt for when you {debt_of} will be repaid "at the right time," and {npc} will know it. You laugh. That winter you are caught in a blizzard on Iron Ridge, lost, with the light going.

choices.text: Dig a snow shelter and wait

ok.log: You dig. You wait. Toward midnight a lantern appears in the snow. It is {npc}, roped to a mule, calling your name.

fail.log: You dig badly. You are nearly gone when the lantern appears. It is {npc}, roped to a mule, calling your name.

choices.text: Keep walking, toward a light you think you see

ok.log: The light is a lantern. The lantern is {npc}, who has been out on the ridge for two days, looking.

fail.log: The light is nothing. You fall. You wake under a blanket, with {npc} chafing your hands.

effects.log: You shout. A voice answers. It is {npc}.

events.text: {npc} has brought you down from Iron Ridge, half frozen, and will not explain how {npc} knew. Now, by the fire in the herder's hut, {npc} finally says: "I have been watching the weather on that ridge every winter since. I knew one day you would be on it."

choices.text: Ask why it mattered so much

effects.log: {npc} looks into the fire. "Because you did not have to do what you did for me. Nobody had ever done anything they did not have to."

choices.text: Say the debt is repaid, many times over

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "Now I can stop watching the weather." {npc} does not stop.
You sleep for a day. When you wake {npc} is still there, mending your boots.

events.text: This winter, {npc} is the one caught on Iron Ridge. A herder brings word: {npc} went up after a lost child, and has not come down. The snow is the worst in twenty years.

mem.note: came up the ridge for me

ok.log: You find them both in a snow hole, the child asleep in {npc}'s coat. You carry the child. {npc} walks, leaning on you.

mem.note: came up the ridge for me

fail.log: You find them. You nearly lose all three of you. The herders find you at dawn in a heap, alive.

choices.text: Rouse the village to search with lanterns

mem.note: sent the village up the ridge

effects.log: Fifty lanterns on the ridge. The child is found first, then {npc}, frostbitten and furious about the fuss.

choices.text: Wait for the snow to stop

effects.log: The snow stops. {npc} walks down with the child, alone, half dead and calm. "I knew the ridge," {npc} says.

events.text: {npc} has become a storyteller in the teahouses of the county town, and announces from the platform, to a full house: "Tonight a free tale, because this one {debt}." {npc} points at you. The whole room turns.

effects.log: The tale is about you, and twice as heroic as the truth. The room cheers. You do not know where to look.
You slip out. The tale is told anyway. People stop you in the street for a week.

choices.text: Stand up and tell it yourself

ok.log: Your version is shorter and funnier. {npc} adds the bits you left out. The room shouts for more.

fail.log: You freeze. {npc} rescues you.

events.text: {npc}'s tale about you has made you a little famous, and a little troubled: a powerful local family thinks the tale is about them, in disguise, and that you are mocking them. They have sent a steward with a polite threat.

choices.text: Go with {npc} to the family and explain

ok.log: The family is mollified, and asks {npc} to tell a tale for the grandmother's birthday.

fail.log: The family is not mollified. {npc} is banned from the best teahouse.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to tell a tale about the family that flatters them

mem.note: asked me to flatter the family

effects.log: {npc} does. It is so flattering it is clearly mockery, and so funny the family laughs too.
The family sends two bruisers. You send them back. The tale gets a sequel.

events.text: {npc} has collected all the tales told in that teahouse over the years into a book, and dedicated it "To the one who started it." The first copy is at your door.

choices.text: Read it all in one night

effects.log: You read until dawn. The last tale is about {npc}, and is the only one in the book that is completely true.

mem.note: came to thank me for the book

effects.log: {npc} is so pleased that a new tale begins on the spot, about a reader who knocked at dawn.

choices.text: Give your copy to the poor school

effects.log: The children of the poor school read it until it falls apart. {npc} sends a box of new copies.

events.text: {npc} arrives with a cart of rice and a wild look. "You {debt}. I would have forgotten. But a ghost came to me in a dream and told me to pay, or it would keep visiting." {npc} unloads the rice very fast.

effects.log: You accept. {npc} sighs with relief and asks if you could sign a receipt, for the ghost.
The ghost was old, had one shoe, and kept asking for pickles. {npc} is sure it was somebody real, from long ago.

choices.text: Say there is no debt, to see what the ghost does

mem.note: would not take the ghost's rice

effects.log: {npc} goes home with the rice. The next morning {npc} is back with the rice, two pickled turnips and a haunted expression.

events.text: {npc}'s ghost has returned in another dream, and is not satisfied. It wants you, specifically, to come and burn incense at a certain grave on the hill behind {npc}'s village. Nobody knows whose grave it is.

mem.note: went to the ghost's grave with me

effects.log: The grave is overgrown, the name worn away. You clean it together and burn incense. That night {npc} sleeps soundly for the first time in a month.

choices.text: Find out whose grave it is first

ok.log: The village register says: a pickle-seller, no family, who once fed two hungry children in a famine. One of them was {npc}.

fail.log: Nobody remembers. You burn incense anyway.

effects.log: {npc} goes alone. The ghost, apparently, is offended with you now.

events.text: {npc} has had no ghost for years. Then a last dream: the ghost, wearing two shoes now, bowing, and saying thank you, and asking for a jar of pickles to be left at your door. {npc} has brought the pickles.

effects.log: They are the best pickles you have ever eaten. You do not ask where {npc} bought them. {npc} does not say.

choices.text: Take the pickles to the grave

mem.note: took the pickles to the grave

effects.log: You leave the jar on the stone. In the morning it is empty. It was probably a fox.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether there was ever a ghost

effects.log: {npc} looks at you for a long time. "Does it matter?"

events.text: {npc} has sewn you a vest of quilted silk, layer on layer, very heavy. "You {debt}. Wear this under your robe. My grandmother sewed one for my grandfather, and it stopped an arrow." It is ugly. It is very warm.

effects.log: It is hot and heavy. You wear it. {npc} checks every time you meet.
You compromise. {npc} disapproves of the summers.

mem.note: put my vest in a cupboard

effects.log: You never wear it. {npc} never asks. You suspect {npc} knows.

events.text: A dart from the dark, in a crowded street. It strikes you square in the back. It does not reach the skin. You stand there, in the middle of the market, with a poisoned dart stuck in the silk of {npc}'s vest.

ok.log: You catch the thrower on a rooftop. A hired killer, very surprised that you are alive.

fail.log: The thrower vanishes. The dart stays in the vest.

mem.note: saw the dart in my vest

effects.log: {npc} looks at the dart and sits down very suddenly.

choices.text: Keep the dart as a lesson

effects.log: You keep it in a box. You never take the vest off again.

events.text: {npc} is going on a long journey through bandit country, and you have had a vest sewn, quilted silk, layer on layer, very heavy, very ugly. You give it to {npc} at the gate.

choices.text: Make {npc} put it on at once

effects.log: {npc} protests and puts it on. A letter comes months later, in a shaky hand: "It stopped a spear. I will never say anything bad about ugly again."

choices.text: Give it, and say nothing more

effects.log: {npc} looks at it a long time and puts it on. You hear nothing for a year, then a short note: "Still wearing it."

choices.text: Ride with {npc} through the bandit country instead

mem.note: rode through the pass with me

ok.log: The vest is not needed. You are.

mem.note: rode through the pass with me

fail.log: The vest is needed. On you.

events.text: {npc} hands you a basket with a lid that moves. "You {debt}. This one is the best of the litter. The mother caught a wolf." The lid comes off. A yellow puppy with one ear up and one ear down falls out and bites your shoe.

effects.log: You call the puppy Shoe. Shoe eats a sandal, a chair leg and a letter from the county office, and sleeps on your feet.

choices.text: Keep the puppy, and name it after {npc}

effects.log: {npc} is outraged and delighted. Every time you call the dog, {npc}, if nearby, answers.
The puppy goes back in the basket and looks at you through the gap with one ear up.

events.text: Shoe the dog, grown large and yellow with one ear still down, has dragged you out of bed at midnight by the sleeve and will not stop barking. The kitchen is on fire.

ok.log: You beat it out with a wet blanket. Shoe stands in the doorway, barking orders.

fail.log: The kitchen burns. You and Shoe stand in the yard. You lose 30 taels of goods, and nothing that matters.

effects.log: The neighbours come with buckets. The kitchen is saved. Shoe accepts a great deal of praise.
{npc} writes back: "I told you. Wolf blood."

events.text: Shoe is very old, grey in the muzzle, and lies all day in the sun by your door. {npc} has come to visit, and Shoe, who has not stood up in a month, stands up, walks to {npc}, and puts a grey head in {npc}'s lap.

effects.log: You sit in the sun all afternoon. Shoe falls asleep between you and does not wake. You bury Shoe under the plum tree.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether there is another litter

effects.log: There is. A month later {npc} brings a basket with a moving lid. The new one has both ears down.
"Thank Shoe's grandmother," says {npc}. "That one caught a wolf." You laugh until Shoe looks offended.

events.text: {npc} sits down opposite you with a brush, an inkstone and a book of old poems. "You {debt}. I cannot fight. But I can teach you to write a poem that will make a magistrate weep. Every evening. For a year."
events.arc: The Clerk Who Taught You Verse

effects.log: The first evening is a disaster. So is the second. On the third you write a line about rain that {npc} reads twice.

choices.text: Agree, if {npc} learns a sword form in return

effects.log: Every evening: a poem, then a sword form. You are both terrible at the other's art, and you both get better.
{npc} closes the book quietly. "Then I will think of something else." {npc} never does.

events.text: {npc}'s poetry lessons have worked too well. You have written a poem about the corrupt grain official that has spread through the county by word of mouth. The official knows who wrote it.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Taught You Verse

effects.log: The official sends a runner. The runner has learned your poem by heart, and recites it to you, and lets you go.

mem.note: asked me to help with the poem

effects.log: {npc} writes a second poem, praising the official so extravagantly that it is clearly mockery. The official cannot arrest a poem of praise.
The official accepts your apology and raises the grain tax. The poem goes on being recited.

events.text: A great poetry gathering in the provincial capital. Your poem about the grain official, years ago, has been chosen to be read. The organisers want the poet to read it. {npc}, who taught you, is in the audience.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Taught You Verse

choices.text: Read it, and say who taught you

effects.log: You read, and at the end you say: "Taught by {npc}, who could not fight." The hall turns. {npc} goes the colour of plums.

ok.log: The new poem is about a clerk and a sword. The hall is silent, then loud. {npc} cannot speak at all.

fail.log: The new poem is clumsy and sincere. The hall is polite. {npc} weeps anyway.

effects.log: {npc} reads it far better than you would. Nobody believes you wrote it.

events.text: {npc} has heard that you and the Gao family have been at each other's throats for years. "You {debt}. I know old Gao. Let me end this." {npc} looks very determined, and very small, next to the size of the quarrel.
events.arc: The Feud That Ended at a Wedding

effects.log: {npc} goes to the Gao house with a pot of tea and does not come out for three days.

mem.note: went to the Gaos with me

effects.log: You go together. Old Gao glares at you over {npc}'s head for an hour without speaking.

choices.text: Refuse: the feud is your affair

mem.note: would not let me end the feud

effects.log: {npc} withdraws. The feud goes on. Sometimes you wonder what would have happened.

events.text: {npc} has done something nobody in the county thought possible: arranged a meeting, at a neutral teahouse, between you and old Gao. You both arrive. Old Gao has brought a knife and a grandchild. {npc} has brought a very large teapot.
events.arc: The Feud That Ended at a Wedding

choices.text: Pour the first cup for Gao

effects.log: Gao looks at the cup a long time, then drinks. The knife stays in its sheath. The grandchild looks at you with frank curiosity.
Gao waits too. {npc} pours for you both, very firmly, and the meeting begins.
Old Gao's face goes through several colours. Then, slowly, Gao apologises too, for the first time in a long life.

events.text: The Gao grandchild who came to the teahouse is getting married, and old Gao has sent an invitation, red, with your name on it. The seat beside yours is for {npc}, "who ended a feud with a teapot."
events.arc: The Feud That Ended at a Wedding

mem.note: sat with me at the Gao wedding

effects.log: Old Gao toasts you. You toast Gao. {npc} sits between you with the teapot and is toasted by everybody.

choices.text: Send a fine gift and go

effects.log: You send a gift worth 30 taels. Old Gao sends back a jar of the Gao family wine, which has never left the house before.

mem.note: asked me to give the speech

effects.log: {npc} gives a speech about teapots. It is the best speech of the wedding.

events.text: {npc} draws a map on the back of your hand with a stick of charcoal. "You {debt}. Behind the abandoned salt store on the east road there is a dry well. Third brick from the top. That silver is mine, honestly. Mostly honestly. It is yours."

ok.log: Third brick from the top. A leather bag of silver. You stand in the well laughing.

fail.log: Third brick: a rat. Fourth brick: a small bag of silver.

effects.log: {npc} explains, at length, a story involving a chess game, a magistrate's cousin and a goat. It is mostly honest.
{npc} sighs. "Fine. I will dig it up and buy you dinner." The dinner is very good.

events.text: Somebody else knew about the dry well behind the salt store: the magistrate's cousin from {npc}'s story, who has come to your door with two large friends to ask about the bag of silver.

effects.log: You hand over what is left, 50 taels. The cousin counts it and leaves, still suspicious.
The cousin goes to {npc}. {npc} does not visit you again for a long time.

choices.text: See the cousin and friends off

ok.log: The large friends are less large lying down. The cousin leaves and does not return.

fail.log: The friends are very large. You pay 30 taels and lose a tooth.

events.text: {npc} has gone straight, and rich, and respectable, and wants to put up a stone at the old dry well behind the salt store, "where everything changed." {npc} asks you to come to the unveiling.

effects.log: The stone says: "Here was nothing. Third brick from the top." Only the two of you understand it.

choices.text: Go, and tell the crowd the story

mem.note: told the story at the well

effects.log: The crowd loves it. {npc} is mortified and pleased.

choices.text: Go, and leave something in the well

effects.log: You leave a single copper behind the third brick from the top, for whoever comes next.

events.text: You are to be flogged at dawn for a brawl that was not your fault, and {npc} has come to the jail at midnight. "You {debt}. The jailer is my uncle, and owes me a favour. I will take your place. Nobody looks at faces in the dark."

choices.text: Refuse: you will take your own punishment

mem.note: refused to let me take your place

effects.log: You take the flogging at dawn. {npc} watches from the crowd with tears in {his} eyes.

mem.note: took your place at the post

effects.log: You walk out into the night. In the morning, {npc} takes ten strokes meant for you.

choices.text: Find another way: talk to the uncle

ok.log: The uncle, persuaded, loses your warrant in a puddle. Nobody is flogged.

fail.log: The uncle will not listen. You take the strokes yourself, and {npc} holds your hand afterwards.

events.text: {npc}'s uncle the jailer has been arrested for selling warrants, and in the uncle's papers is the record of the night of the swap. The magistrate wants to know who walked out of that jail.

effects.log: You confess. The magistrate, amused by honesty from a strange quarter, fines you lightly and lets {npc} go.
