The magistrate never finds out. {npc}'s uncle takes the blame for everything.

choices.text: Pay the magistrate to close the matter

effects.log: You pay 60 taels. The matter is closed. You feel worse than after any flogging.

events.text: {npc} has become a jailer, of all things, in the county jail where you once sat waiting for the post. It is the most humane jail in the province: no beatings, clean straw, letters allowed. {npc} asks you to come and see it.

effects.log: {npc} shows you the cell where you sat. There is a sign on it: "Nobody is flogged here for a brawl they did not start."
You bring 20 taels of blankets. {npc} hands them out and tells every prisoner who sent them.

mem.note: asked why I became a jailer

effects.log: "Because of a night when somebody walked out of one," {npc} says, "and I saw what it meant."

events.text: {npc} has bought a small inn at the crossroads of the four counties, and has a promise for you: "You {debt}. The east room on the top floor is yours. Always. It will be kept empty for you, every night, whether you come or not."

effects.log: You stay the first night. The east room has a view of three roads and a bed someone has clearly fussed over.

choices.text: Insist {npc} rent the room to others

mem.note: told me to rent the room

effects.log: {npc} refuses. "It is empty for you. That is the point." The room stays empty.

mem.note: said the room was too much

effects.log: "It is one room," says {npc}. "I have eleven."

events.text: A storm, a broken axle and a long night: you arrive at the crossroads inn at midnight, soaked, unannounced. The inn is full, every bed taken, merchants sleeping on tables. The east room on the top floor is empty, a lamp lit, the bed turned down.

effects.log: You sleep like a stone. In the morning {npc} has breakfast waiting and pretends it was no trouble.

choices.text: Give the room to a family sleeping on the stairs

effects.log: The family is astonished. You sleep on a table. {npc} finds out and is furious, then proud.

choices.text: Ask how long the lamp has been lit

effects.log: "Every night," says {npc}. "Seven years." You do not know what to say.

events.text: {npc} is old and selling the crossroads inn. The new owner has agreed to every condition but one: the east room. {npc} has written to ask what you want done with it.

choices.text: Ask that the room be kept for travellers in need

effects.log: The room becomes the Room for Whoever Comes in a Storm. {npc} paints the sign.

choices.text: Ask that it be kept for {npc}

effects.log: {npc} lives out the last years in the east room, with a view of three roads.
The room is rented. {npc} writes: "Somebody is sleeping in your bed. I hope they are cold."

events.text: {npc} has risen at court, and has written you a letter of recommendation, sealed with an official seal. "You {debt}. Take this to the examination hall in the capital. They will read your papers twice." It is a door, and doors are dangerous.

choices.text: Go to the capital with the letter

effects.log: You travel to the capital. The examination hall is enormous. The letter, when you show it, makes a clerk sit up very straight.

choices.text: Go, but do not use the letter

ok.log: You pass on your own merit, near the top. {npc} is half offended, half delighted.

fail.log: You fail. You keep the letter in your sleeve all the way home, unused, and do not regret it.

choices.text: Burn the letter: favours at court are poison

effects.log: You burn it. {npc} hears and is hurt, and does not write for a year.

events.text: The examiner who read your papers twice because of {npc}'s letter has been accused of favouritism, and the letter has been found. {npc} is under investigation. A court official has come to ask about your papers.

choices.text: Tell the official the truth: you would have passed anyway

mem.note: spoke for me to the court

ok.log: The official reads your papers and agrees. The case against {npc} is dropped.

fail.log: The official is not convinced. {npc} is demoted but not dismissed.

choices.text: Offer to sit the examination again, in public

mem.note: sat the exam again for me

effects.log: You sit it again in front of the court. You pass. The case collapses.
{npc} is dismissed. You keep your place. It does not feel like yours.

events.text: {npc} is in exile, in a small town on the southern coast, after a court quarrel that had nothing to do with you. The letter says: "The fishing is good. The magistrate is a fool. I am happy. Visit if you can."

effects.log: You fish together for a month. {npc} has never looked so well. You envy {npc} a little.

ok.log: The petition succeeds. {npc} writes: "Thank you. Please do not do that again. The fishing was good."

fail.log: The petition fails. {npc} writes to say thank you, and that the fishing is still good.

effects.log: You send 10 taels of tea. {npc} sends back dried fish.

events.text: {npc} holds out a plain jade ring on a red cord. "You {debt}. This was my grandmother's, the only good thing I ever owned. I pawned it in a bad winter and have spent three years buying it back from the Wang pawnshop. Now it is yours."

effects.log: It is warm from {npc}'s hand. You wear it on the cord, and it never seems to get cold.

choices.text: Ask what it cost to redeem

effects.log: {npc} will not say. You find out later from the pawnbroker: three months of {npc}'s wages.
{npc} wears it, from then on, on the red cord, every day.

events.text: Old Wang the pawnbroker, who held the ring all those years, has gone bankrupt, and the pawnshop's other tickets are worthless. Dozens of the poor have lost their last good things. {npc} has come to tell you, and has a plan.

choices.text: Help {npc} buy back the pawnshop's stock

mem.note: bought back the pawned things with me

effects.log: You pay 80 taels between you and return every pawned thing to its owner. A grandmother gets back a hairpin and weeps for an hour.

choices.text: Find the pawnbroker's creditors and negotiate

ok.log: The creditors agree to release the pledges for a fraction. The poor get their things back.

fail.log: The creditors agree to release half. It is half.

effects.log: {npc} manages a little. The rest is lost.

events.text: {npc}, who once spent three years redeeming a ring, has opened an honest pawnshop for the poor of the quarter: low interest, long terms, no shame. The sign is a jade ring on a red cord.

effects.log: You pay 50 taels. {npc} gives you a ticket for it. "In case you ever need it back."

choices.text: Pawn something to be the first customer

effects.log: You pawn a kettle for a copper. {npc} puts it in the window as an advertisement.
You stand in front of it for a long time. It is a good sign.

events.text: {npc} has inherited a tea estate in the southern hills, small and steep and overgrown, and has written you into the deed: "You {debt}. One tenth of every harvest is yours, as long as the bushes grow." The first harvest arrives: one small sack.

effects.log: It is wonderful tea, rough and green and smelling of hills. You drink it slowly.

choices.text: Go and help with the second harvest

effects.log: You spend a month on the slopes picking leaves. Your back will never be the same. The tea is better for it.
It sells for 15 taels. {npc} sends the next sack anyway, with a note: "Drink this one."

events.text: {npc}'s tea estate has been struck by a blight. The bushes are dying. {npc} has written in despair: one tenth of nothing, the letter says, is still nothing, and {npc} is sorry.

choices.text: Go south and fight the blight together

mem.note: saved the tea estate with me

ok.log: You find a herbalist who knows the blight. You burn and replant together. In two years, the slopes are green again.

fail.log: The blight wins half the slope. The other half lives.

effects.log: You send 50 taels. New bushes go in. The harvest is small for three years and then, suddenly, wonderful.

choices.text: Write that the debt is paid

effects.log: {npc} writes back: "Not for you to say." A small sack arrives the next year, half blighted, sent anyway.

events.text: The tea from {npc}'s estate has been chosen as tribute tea for the imperial court. The estate is famous. One tenth of every harvest is now a great deal of tea.

effects.log: Your tenth is worth 120 taels this year. You put most of it aside for a lean year.

choices.text: Give your share back to the pickers

effects.log: The pickers, who have been paid little for a long time, are paid well this year. {npc} follows your example.

choices.text: Ask for a small sack, as at first

effects.log: {npc} sends one small sack, rough and green and smelling of hills, and a note: "Same as the first."

events.text: {npc} has come to you with a strange offer. "You {debt}. I am at the end of my road. I will never break through. But I have forty years of cultivation. I can give you some of it, palm to back, if you will take it."

effects.log: You sit back to back. Warmth flows into you like a river. {npc} is pale and smiling when it is done.
{npc} looks at you a long time. "Then use your own," {npc} says, "and break through for both of us."
A small flow, carefully held. {npc} is a little disappointed and a little relieved.

events.text: The cultivation {npc} gave you has settled into your meridians and made the next wall look thinner. You are going into seclusion to break through. {npc} has asked to sit outside the door.

effects.log: You can feel {npc} outside, steady as a stone. On the forty-ninth night the wall breaks.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to come in and guide you

ok.log: {npc}'s hand on your back again, guiding the qi through the old channel. The wall breaks like ice in spring.

fail.log: The guidance is not enough. You come out tired and unbroken, and {npc} apologises for an hour.

effects.log: You go to the mountains. When you come back stronger, {npc} is waiting at the gate.

events.text: {npc} is old and weak, and the gift has cost more than {npc} said. You have broken through, and there is a way, the old manuals say, to give some back: palm to back, the other direction.

effects.log: You sit back to back. The river flows the other way. {npc} weeps. You feel lighter, not weaker.
You pay 60 taels for a longevity pill. {npc} takes it and lives ten more years, grumbling.
{npc} thinks. "Teach someone what I taught you." You take a student that spring.

events.text: {npc} opens a small ledger bound in blue cloth. Every page is about you. "You {debt}. I have written down what it was worth, and every repayment since. I am behind." The ledger lists, among other things, a bowl of noodles, a kind word, and "the business with the goose."

effects.log: The totals are in three columns: silver, kindness and "other". The "other" column is the longest.

choices.text: Ask what the business with the goose was

effects.log: {npc} tells you. You had forgotten. You laugh until you have to sit down.

choices.text: Take the ledger and burn it

effects.log: {npc} watches the ledger burn with real grief, and starts a new one that evening, from memory.

events.text: {npc} has made an entry in the blue ledger that worries you: "Owed: one life. Repayment pending." You have heard that someone has been asking questions about you in the wine shops, someone with a grudge.

effects.log: {npc} closes the ledger. "It means I am watching your back. Do not argue."

choices.text: Find the person asking questions yourself

roll.foeName: the hired sword asking about you

ok.log: You find the hired sword in the third wine shop. The conversation is short. {npc} crosses out the entry, disappointed.

fail.log: The hired sword is good. You only just win. {npc} bandages you and writes "pending" again.

effects.log: The questions stop. You never learn how. The entry in the ledger reads "Paid" in red ink.

events.text: {npc} brings you the blue ledger, finished. On the last page, under all the columns, is a single line in a steadier hand than the rest: "Balance: even. Friendship: continuing."

choices.text: Start a ledger of your own

effects.log: You buy a blue notebook. The first entry is the business with the goose.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep the ledger going

effects.log: {npc} is delighted. A second volume begins, entirely in the "other" column.

choices.text: Keep the ledger as a treasure

effects.log: It sits on your shelf beside your best things. On bad days you read about the goose.

events.text: {npc} has spent a year embroidering a banner for you: a white crane over red waves, your name in gold thread. "You {debt}. Every fighter of the old days had a banner. Now you do." It is enormous. It is, you realise, meant to be carried.

effects.log: It fills a whole wall. Visitors ask about it. You tell them about {npc}.

choices.text: Carry it into the next fight

effects.log: You carry it up the mountain road against the bandits of the pass. The bandits, seeing a banner, think you are an army, and leave.
{npc} rolls it up, crushed, then unrolls it again. "Too grand is the point."

events.text: A flood has swept away the village by the river, and the survivors are on the hill with nothing. They need a sign, something to rally to, so people from the scattered farms know where to come. {npc} brings you the crane banner.

choices.text: Raise the banner on the hill

effects.log: The crane flies over the hill for a month. People come in from the farms. The village rebuilds under it.
The gold thread itches, but forty children sleep warm. {npc} says it is the best thing the banner could have been.
You send 40 taels. The banner stays on your wall. The village rebuilds, slowly.

events.text: The village on the river, rebuilt, has made a festival of the day the crane banner went up on the hill. They have woven a new one, and want you and {npc} to carry it at the head of the procession.

effects.log: It is heavy. You carry it the whole way, one pole each, and do not let go.

choices.text: Let the village children carry it

effects.log: Six children carry the banner, staggering, beaming. You and {npc} walk behind and catch it when it tips.

choices.text: Ask that {npc}'s name be added in gold

mem.note: added my name to the banner

effects.log: It is. {npc} spends the whole festival looking at it.

events.text: {npc}, who was once an actor in a travelling troupe, has come to repay you with the one thing {npc} knows. "You {debt}. I will teach you to be somebody else. Faces, voices, walks. Nobody will ever find you if you do not want to be found."

effects.log: In a month you can be an old fishmonger, a young monk and a tired clerk. Your own neighbours walk past you.
The walk is the secret, {npc} says. People see a walk before a face. You learn to walk like ten people.

choices.text: Decline: you are happy being yourself

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Rare. Good. Stay that way."

events.text: You are being hunted: a powerful enemy has put a price on you, and there are hired eyes at every gate of the city. {npc} has come with a bundle. "Now you see why I taught you."

choices.text: Walk out of the city as a fishmonger

ok.log: You walk out past six hired eyes with a basket of fish. One of them buys a carp.

fail.log: A hired eye looks twice. You run, and {npc} trips the watcher with a cart.

choices.text: Stay and use the disguise to find the enemy

ok.log: As a tired clerk you walk into the enemy's counting house and out again with the ledger that ruins them.

fail.log: The disguise holds. The enemy does not show. You leave the city anyway.

effects.log: You travel three provinces as the troupe's third ghost. You are a terrible actor. Nobody suspects a thing.

events.text: {npc} is old, and the troupe is putting on one last show, and wants you, the third ghost, to play your old part.

mem.note: played the ghost one last time

effects.log: You forget your lines. The audience thinks it is part of the play. {npc} weeps with laughter in the wings.

choices.text: Play {npc}'s old part, as a tribute

effects.log: You play it in {npc}'s walk. The old actors in the audience gasp. {npc} watches from the front row, very still.

mem.note: sat in the audience with me

effects.log: You watch the show together. {npc} mouths every line, and corrects the lead actor afterwards.

events.text: There is a sack on your doorstep, tied with red ribbon. In the sack is a bandit chief, gagged, furious. Pinned to the sack is a note from {npc}: "You {debt}. This is the one who burned the mill road. Do as you like."

choices.text: Take the bandit chief to the magistrate

effects.log: The magistrate pays the bounty of 50 taels and asks, faintly, how it was done. You show the ribbon.

choices.text: Untie the bandit chief and ask questions

effects.log: The bandit tells you who paid for the mill road burning. It was not a bandit's idea at all.
{npc} writes back: "I did not know what else you would like. Ducks seemed small."

events.text: The bandit chief from the sack has escaped the magistrate's jail and is out for revenge, not on you, but on {npc}, who did the sacking. {npc} has sent word: "I may have made a small mistake."

mem.note: stood with me against the gang

ok.log: The gang comes at night. You and {npc} meet them at the gate. By dawn there is a second sack, and a longer ribbon.

fail.log: The gang is beaten off, at a price. {npc} sews your wounds and apologises for the ribbon.

effects.log: {npc} lives in your attic for a month, complaining. The gang gives up and moves on.

choices.text: Find out who paid for the mill road

ok.log: The one behind the mill road is a grain merchant. Once the merchant is arrested, the gang has no paymaster, and drifts away.

fail.log: You find nothing. The gang finds {npc}'s house empty.

events.text: The bandit chief from the sack, after years on the river dykes, has turned up at {npc}'s door with a sack of sweet potatoes tied with a red ribbon, and has asked to see you both. "I have come to say I deserved the sack," the old bandit says. "And to ask for work."

mem.note: gave the bandit work with me

effects.log: The old bandit guards {npc}'s warehouse for twenty years. Nothing is ever stolen. Nobody dares.

choices.text: Ask the old bandit to teach the village youths to fight

effects.log: The youths of the village become very good at fighting and very bad at being robbed.
The old bandit leaves the sweet potatoes on the step anyway. They are very good sweet potatoes.

events.text: {npc}, who gathers herbs for a living, has come with a rope over one shoulder. "You {debt}. On the north face of Jade Screen Peak there is a red cloud-herb that flowers once in thirty years. This is the year. I know where. Nobody else does."

mem.note: climbed Jade Screen Peak with me

effects.log: You climb for four days. Above the clouds the air is thin and the silence is enormous. {npc} points to a ledge.
{npc} goes alone and is gone a week. You worry the whole time.

choices.text: Refuse: it is too dangerous for {npc}

effects.log: {npc} sighs and coils the rope. "Thirty years," {npc} says. "I will be too old next time."

events.text: The red cloud-herb is on a ledge below an overhang on Jade Screen Peak, glowing like a coal. Someone must go down on the rope and someone must hold it. {npc} looks at you. "I am lighter. You are stronger."

choices.text: Hold the rope while {npc} goes down

mem.note: held the rope on Jade Screen

ok.log: The rope burns your palms raw. {npc} comes up with the herb in {his} teeth, laughing. You share it on the summit.

mem.note: held the rope on Jade Screen

fail.log: The rope slips a hand's width and {npc} swings out over the void. You hold. The herb comes up crushed but whole.

ok.log: You hang over the clouds and pluck the herb. {npc} hauls you up, white-faced.

fail.log: The overhang crumbles. You come up with half the herb and a cracked rib.

effects.log: You sit on the ledge and watch it open. In thirty years, it will seed the whole face.

events.text: {npc} is ill with a wasting fever that no physician can touch. Only something like the red cloud-herb of Jade Screen Peak could help, and its next flowering is twenty-four years away.

choices.text: Search the peak for a second plant

ok.log: Three weeks on the north face. Under the overhang, a seedling has flowered early, only one flower. You bring it down.

fail.log: You find nothing. On the way down you find a hermit with a jar of dried cloud-herb, who gives you a pinch for the tale.

choices.text: Give {npc} what you kept from that day

effects.log: You kept a single dried petal in a box, for luck. You put it in {npc}'s tea. The fever breaks.

mem.note: sat with me in the fever

effects.log: You sit and talk about the peak. The fever breaks on the seventh day, by itself, as fevers sometimes do.

events.text: {npc}, a boatwright on the river, has built you a boat: small, quick, painted green, with the name Thanks on the bow in clumsy characters. "You {debt}. On the river a boat is freedom."

effects.log: You row upriver at dawn, through mist, past fishermen who wave. You understand what {npc} meant.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to teach you the river

effects.log: {npc} teaches you the currents, the shoals and the moods of the water. It takes all summer.
You sell it for 30 taels. You see it on the river sometimes, with another name.

events.text: River pirates have been robbing the ferries below the gorges. The river guard is too slow. {npc} says the green boat called Thanks is the fastest on the river, and asks if you would like to do something about the pirates.

choices.text: Hunt the pirates in Thanks with {npc}

mem.note: hunted pirates in Thanks with me

ok.log: Thanks flies across the gorge. The pirates do not expect a small green boat to attack. Three are caught. The rest are never seen again.

fail.log: The pirates hole Thanks below the line. You swim ashore together, furious, and catch them the next week on foot.

choices.text: Carry the river guard in Thanks

effects.log: Thanks carries four guards fast enough to catch the pirates in the act. You are thanked, a little.
The pirates go on robbing. {npc} goes out alone in another boat, and comes back with a pirate tied in the bilge.

events.text: Thanks, the green boat, is old and leaking and patched in eleven places. {npc} has offered to build you a new one. "It will be faster. It will not leak. It will have a better name."

choices.text: Ask {npc} to mend the old one instead

effects.log: {npc} spends a month on it. Thanks comes back with twelve patches and a new coat of green.
The new boat is called Thanks Again. It is faster. You miss the old leaks.
Thanks sits on the bank by your door and fills with flowers. {npc} paints it every spring.

events.text: {npc} has heard the rumour going round about you, the one about the stolen silver at the Lu manor, which is not true. "You {debt}. Rumours die when somebody kills them. I am going to kill this one."

effects.log: {npc} goes from teahouse to teahouse. Within a month the rumour has been replaced by a better one, about a goat.

choices.text: Ask how {npc} plans to do it

effects.log: The plan is simple. A bigger rumour, a funnier one, about the person who started the first one.
{npc} leaves it alone. The rumour dies by itself, in its own time. It takes four years.

events.text: The rumour {npc} killed has been traced back to its source, a merchant with a grudge, who has now started a rumour about {npc}. It is worse. It is about {npc}'s family.

ok.log: You confront the merchant in front of the guild. The merchant, caught, apologises to {npc} in public. Both rumours die.

fail.log: The merchant laughs at you both. The guild, though, does not.

ok.log: You find the truth and spread it, carefully. Within a month, the merchant's own guild is asking questions.

fail.log: The new rumour is stubborn. It fades, slowly.

effects.log: You pay 50 taels. The merchant stops. You suspect the merchant will start again when the silver runs out.

events.text: The merchant who spread both rumours has gone bankrupt, and is begging at the temple gate. {npc} has come to you, troubled. "I wanted the rumours to die. I did not want this."

choices.text: Give the merchant food and work

effects.log: The merchant weeps. In a year the merchant is honest, poor and useful, and once tells you the truth about a bad deal.
You walk past. {npc} does not. {npc} buys the merchant a meal every day for a month.

mem.note: told me it was not my fault

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. Then goes to the temple gate with a bowl of rice anyway.

events.text: {npc} has ridden down from the northern grasslands with a black horse on a lead rope, a horse taller than any you have seen. "You {debt}. In the north we pay debts with horses. This is the best one I have ever raised. The name is Night Wind."

effects.log: Night Wind looks at you as an equal. You will spend a year earning the right to ride.

ok.log: You stay on. Night Wind takes you across three fields at a speed that empties your head of every thought.

fail.log: Night Wind puts you in the river. {npc} laughs so hard that {npc} falls off {his} own horse.

choices.text: Refuse: a horse like that should stay in the north

effects.log: {npc} looks at you with new respect and rides home with the horse.

events.text: War on the border. Night Wind the black horse, who has lived in your stable for four years and thinks it is a grassland, has started pulling at the rope toward the north every night.

ok.log: You reach {npc}'s camp in seven days. Night Wind carries you through the raiders like a black wind. The border holds.

fail.log: You arrive in time to be wounded in the first charge. {npc} carries you out of the battle across Night Wind's saddle.

choices.text: Let Night Wind go north alone

effects.log: You take off the rope. Night Wind goes north. Months later, a letter: "The horse found me. I knew you would understand."

choices.text: Keep Night Wind in the stable

effects.log: You tie the rope tighter. Night Wind stops eating for a week. You never quite feel you did right.

events.text: Night Wind is old, and {npc} has come down from the north to see the old horse once more. The horse lifts its grey head at {npc}'s voice, and the three of you stand in the stable yard in silence.

mem.note: rode out together one last time

effects.log: Slowly, to the river and back. Night Wind is very old. Night Wind is very happy.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to take Night Wind home to die on the grass

effects.log: {npc} leads the old horse north. A letter comes in the spring: Night Wind died on the open grass with the wind in its mane.

choices.text: Ask {npc} for a foal of Night Wind's line

mem.note: brought a foal of the line

effects.log: The next spring a black foal comes south with {npc}. It bites you at once. It is perfect.

events.text: {npc}, a scholar who failed the examinations three times, has a talent for writing petitions. "You {debt}. Your village pays a salt tax that was abolished ten years ago. I will write to the prefect." {npc} has already started.

effects.log: The petition is eleven pages long, polite, lethal. {npc} reads it aloud to you twice.

choices.text: Help {npc} gather the old tax rolls

effects.log: You spend a month in dusty records. The proof is there: the tax was abolished, and someone has been keeping it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to leave it: officials take revenge

effects.log: {npc} folds up the petition. You see it, years later, still folded, in {npc}'s desk.

events.text: The petition about the false salt tax has reached the prefect, and the prefect has ordered an inquiry. The county tax collector, who has been pocketing the tax, has had {npc} arrested on a false charge.

mem.note: went to the prefect for me

ok.log: The prefect hears you out and orders {npc} freed and the tax collector arrested. The village gets ten years of salt tax back.

mem.note: went to the prefect for me

fail.log: The prefect is away. {npc} sits in jail for a month before the inquiry frees {npc}.

ok.log: You get {npc} out over the wall. Now you are both outlaws, briefly, until the inquiry clears {npc}.

fail.log: You fall off the wall. The guards laugh. {npc} is freed a month later anyway.

effects.log: Three hundred villagers sit outside the tax office. {npc} is freed by nightfall.

events.text: {npc}'s petition is now famous in the province: a model of its kind, copied by students. {npc} has finally passed the examination, on the fourth try, and been appointed a county magistrate. The first case on the new magistrate's desk is a petition from your village.

choices.text: Ask what the petition is about

mem.note: read the village petition with me

effects.log: It is a thank-you letter, signed by every family in the village, asking the new magistrate to come to the spring festival.
{npc} is sworn in. Afterwards, out of habit, {npc} writes a petition to the new magistrate about the road.

choices.text: Send a brush as a gift

effects.log: A good brush, 10 taels. {npc} writes every judgement with it for thirty years.

events.text: {npc} has come back after many years of wandering, older, browner and with a pack full of strange things. "You {debt}. I have carried this debt across eleven provinces. I have brought you a present from every one."

effects.log: A seashell, a bag of red pepper, a rusty bell, a carved bear, a feather from a bird nobody has a name for. You stay up all night hearing where each one came from.
{npc} talks about the far west, the deserts, the great salt lakes, the mountains that hold up the sky. You listen until the lamp runs out.
{npc} is moved. "A while," {npc} says. It is a long while.

events.text: {npc} the wanderer is restless again. The pack is on the floor. The road is calling. But this time {npc} has asked you to come, for one journey, to see one of the eleven provinces together.

ok.log: You walk west for half a year. You see the great salt lake. You come home different.

fail.log: The road is hard. You fall ill in the mountains. {npc} nurses you, and you see the lake anyway.

effects.log: {npc} goes alone. Letters come, from far away, with a feather or a shell inside.
You give {npc} your best knife. "Leave it somewhere beautiful." {npc} sends a drawing of where.

events.text: A parcel comes from the far west, sewn in leather, with no letter. Inside are the eleven presents you were once given, a twelfth from somewhere new, and your old knife. The traveller who brought it says {npc} died on the road, smiling, in a high pass.

effects.log: You walk for two months. In the high pass is a cairn of stones with a seashell on top. You add your knife.

choices.text: Keep the presents together on a shelf

effects.log: Twelve strange things on a shelf. Visitors ask. You tell them about {npc}.

choices.text: Give the presents away, one each, to children who want to travel

effects.log: Twelve children, twelve presents. You hope some of them go far.

events.text: {npc} has taken up painting, and has painted you, from memory, as repayment. "You {debt}. Now you will be remembered." The portrait is enormous. Your nose is wrong. Your expression is that of someone about to sneeze heroically.
events.arc: The Portrait You Did Not Sit For

effects.log: Visitors stop in front of it and look from it to you and back. A child bursts into tears. You love it.

choices.text: Offer to sit properly for a second one

effects.log: You sit for a month. The second portrait is better. Your nose is still wrong, in a different way.
You roll it up and put it in a chest. {npc} visits often and looks at the walls.

events.text: {npc}'s painting has improved beyond recognition. A great collector has seen the old sneezing portrait of you and wants to buy it, at an absurd price, as "the earliest work of a master."
events.arc: The Portrait You Did Not Sit For

choices.text: Sell it, and give {npc} the silver

effects.log: {npc} uses the silver to open a painting school. The first lesson is noses.
You refuse the collector. {npc} pretends to be annoyed and is visibly delighted.

choices.text: Sell it and keep the silver

effects.log: You get 150 taels. {npc} says nothing. The next portrait {npc} sends you is of a goose.

events.text: {npc}, now a famous painter, is old, and has painted a last portrait of you: true, this time, the nose exactly right. "I owed you a face," says the inscription. "Now you have one."
events.arc: The Portrait You Did Not Sit For

choices.text: Hang the two portraits side by side

effects.log: The sneezing hero and the true face, side by side. Visitors prefer the first. So do you.

choices.text: Give the last portrait to a temple

effects.log: The monks hang it in the hall of benefactors. You go to look at it sometimes, and it looks back.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to paint a self-portrait, for you

effects.log: {npc} paints it in a week. It is the only time {npc} ever paints {his} own face, and the nose is wrong.

events.text: {npc} has paid the Temple of the White Horse to carve your name on its tablet of merit, among the names of generals and great ministers. "You {debt}. Now the monks will pray for you every day." Your name is the smallest on the tablet and the newest.
events.arc: The Name on the Merit Tablet

effects.log: Your name sits between a dead general and a living salt merchant. An old monk tells you who everyone was.

choices.text: Pay for {npc}'s name to be carved too

effects.log: You pay 20 taels. The monks carve {npc}'s name beside yours, the newest of all.

choices.text: Ask that the name be taken down

mem.note: asked to take the name down

effects.log: The abbot refuses: the merit is paid for. {npc} is hurt, and does not visit you for a season.

events.text: The Temple of the White Horse is falling down. The monks have come to everyone on the merit tablet to ask for help with the roof. Most of the names are long dead. {npc} has already given everything {npc} had.
events.arc: The Name on the Merit Tablet

effects.log: You pay 60 taels. The roof is mended. The abbot moves your name, with great ceremony, three places higher.

choices.text: Go and mend the roof yourself, with {npc}

mem.note: mended the temple roof with me

effects.log: You and {npc} spend a month on the roof with the monks, tiling. The old monk calls you "the two who climbed."
You give 10 taels. {npc} is quietly disappointed.

events.text: The old monk of the White Horse temple has died, and in the old monk's cell they found a small book of prayers, one for each name on the merit tablet. Yours is the longest. The abbot thinks you should have it, since {npc} asked the monk to write it.
events.arc: The Name on the Merit Tablet

effects.log: It is a prayer for someone the monk never met, written from everything {npc} told the old monk. It is the best description of you that exists.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read it to you

effects.log: {npc} reads it in a cracked voice. Halfway through, you both start to laugh at the part about the goose.
You ask the monks to keep praying it. They do, every morning, for a long time.

events.text: {npc} has found the bandit who once robbed you on the mountain road, and has brought the bandit to you, tied and on foot. "You {debt}. This is yours to judge." The bandit is thin and grey and looks at the ground.

choices.text: Take the bandit to the magistrate

effects.log: The magistrate sends the bandit to the dykes. {npc} looks satisfied. You feel strangely little.
You cut the ropes. {npc} stares at you. The bandit runs, then stops, then bows to the ground, then runs.
The bandit had three children and a failed harvest. It is a very ordinary story.

events.text: The bandit you judged is back. Not robbing: farming, on a small plot by the river, with three grown children. The bandit has sent you a sack of rice, and {npc} a sack of rice, and a letter for you both, written by one of the children.

choices.text: Go and visit the farm with {npc}

mem.note: visited the bandit's farm with me

effects.log: The old bandit cooks for you. The children stare at the two people who decided their parent's fate.
The rice is good. You do not quite know what to feel.
The rice comes back again, with another letter, more insistent.

events.text: The old bandit's eldest child has passed the county examination, the first from that river, and has asked you and {npc} to the celebration, as "the two who gave my family a second road."

effects.log: The old bandit weeps through the whole feast. {npc} gives a speech about mercy that makes you cringe and agree.

choices.text: Send a brush for the young scholar

effects.log: A good brush, 10 taels. The young scholar writes the first judgement with it, years later, as a magistrate, and it is merciful.

choices.text: Stay away: it is their day

effects.log: You stay away. {npc} goes, and tells you everything, at length.

events.text: {npc} is poor, and has nothing to give but work. "You {debt}. I will make you straw sandals. Ten pairs a year, as long as I can plait." The first ten pairs are stacked at your door, very neat.

effects.log: They are the best sandals you have ever worn: light, tight, silent on a roof. You understand why your feet ached before.

mem.note: gave my sandals to the poor

effects.log: Ten beggars in the market walk better this winter. {npc} plaits faster.
You leave 10 taels. {npc} brings twenty pairs next year, out of offence.

events.text: You have walked a very long way in {npc}'s sandals: to the coast, to the mountains, across a desert of red sand. This year {npc}'s ten pairs come with a note: "My hands are getting stiff. These may be the last good ones."

effects.log: {npc} teaches you, patiently, for a week. Your first pair falls apart. Your tenth does not.

mem.note: sent a physician for my hands

effects.log: The physician's ointment helps. The sandals keep coming.

choices.text: Write that the debt is long since paid

effects.log: {npc} writes back: "I know. It stopped being a debt a long time ago."

events.text: You have plaited your own straw sandals for years now, as {npc} taught you. This year you make ten pairs and carry them to {npc}'s door, very neat.

choices.text: Leave them at the door, and knock

effects.log: {npc} opens the door, sees the sandals and laughs until coughing. "The plaiting is too loose on the left." It is.
You plait all afternoon, side by side, not saying much. It is the best afternoon of the year.
The next morning, the left plait on every pair has been tightened. Ten pairs come back to you, corrected.

events.text: {npc} sits down across from you with paper and a brush. "You {debt}. I can do one thing well: read and write. I will teach you, an hour a night, until you can write a letter to anybody in the world."

effects.log: The first week your characters look like spiders in a fight. By the third month they look like spiders at a festival. It is progress.

choices.text: Learn, and teach {npc} a fighting stance in exchange

effects.log: An hour of brush, an hour of stance. {npc} falls over a great deal. You blot a great deal.

choices.text: Say you already read well enough

effects.log: {npc} nods and goes. You find a book left on your step, with the hard characters underlined.

events.text: Your first real letter, written in your own hand after {npc}'s lessons, has been sent: to a magistrate, about a crooked tax. The magistrate has written back. The reply is in an official hand you can actually read, and it says the tax will be looked into.

effects.log: {npc} reads it three times, then frames it. "My first student to win a case."
You write about a broken dyke. That one is answered too. You begin to understand what {npc} gave you.

choices.text: Write to {npc} instead, a real letter

effects.log: You write to {npc}, though {npc} lives across the street. {npc} writes back. It becomes a habit.

events.text: {npc} is ill, and can no longer read: the eyes have gone. A servant has come to ask if you would read {npc}'s letters aloud, "since you were taught."

effects.log: An hour a night, as once it was the other way. You read letters, then poems, then the old lessons, which {npc} still corrects.

choices.text: Find a young student to read

effects.log: You find a bright child from the market and teach the child to read, so the child can read to {npc}.

choices.text: Write {npc} a long letter and read it aloud

effects.log: The letter is about the lessons, the spiders, the tax and the dyke. {npc} listens with closed eyes and smiles at every mistake.

events.text: {npc}, now a grain merchant, takes you aside at the market. "You {debt}. Listen: the river dykes are rotten. Somebody has been stealing the repair silver for years. When the spring flood comes they will go. Move anything you love to high ground."

effects.log: You move what you can to the hill. You feel foolish all winter.
{npc} lowers the voice. A name: the dyke commissioner's own nephew.
You laugh. The spring comes. You remember {npc}'s face.

events.text: The spring flood is coming, and the dykes are as rotten as {npc} said. The dyke commissioner's nephew, who stole the repair silver, has fled. The county has three days.

choices.text: Organise the village to shore up the dykes

mem.note: shored up the dykes with me

ok.log: Three days of sandbags, every hand in the county, {npc} hauling sacks beside you. The dykes hold, barely.

fail.log: You shore up two dykes. The third goes. Most of the county is saved.

effects.log: The dykes break. The fields drown. Nobody does.

ok.log: You catch the nephew at the ferry with the silver. It is too late for the dykes, but not for the repair.

fail.log: The nephew escapes. The dykes break.

events.text: New dykes stand along the river, built with the recovered silver and honest hands. The county has asked {npc}, whose warning saved it, to become the new dyke commissioner. {npc} has asked you what to do.

mem.note: told me to take the post

effects.log: {npc} takes it. The dykes are inspected every month, publicly, with the accounts read aloud in the market.
You walk the dykes every spring with a stick, poking. {npc} reads the accounts. The river behaves.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to refuse: posts change people

effects.log: {npc} refuses. The new commissioner is honest anyway. {npc} watches closely, just in case.
